subsubtopic: RESULT OF LIBERAL PARTY LEADERSHIP CAMPAIGN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thinking that the Liberal Party still retains some vestige of collective intelligence, I had so wagered on the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) last weekend. However, the death wish was amongst them and they disregarded the one candidate who might have stood them one small chance of success in the next election.
Doomed to failure with a Leader whose first act as the Prime Minister designate was to impose closure on the security Bill, therefore showing his disdain for Canadians and the institution of Parliament, the Liberals struggle manfully on to the oblivion that awaits them at the polls. subsubtopic: LIBERAL PARTY LEADERSHIP CONVENTION-ROLE OF EDMONTON MAYOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, westerners are proud people of honour who believe that a handshake agreement is a contractual bond. Then the bomb arrived. The true Grit Edmonton mayor who nominated the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) for Leader of the Liberal Party did a 100-yard dash to self-serving safety, right in the middle of round one. Commitment and loyalty were consumed by nervousness. The mayor's Liberal instinct was to seek power with honour if necessary, but not necessarily an honourable power. His was a buddy system that left his friend choking in the water while he climbed into a new self-preservation suit. What may we expect of a person who so openly betrays a friend? Would this person also pretend to oppose wage and price controls, or fool people into believing that we could have cheap
gasoline in spite of world price, or speak with a forked tongue about co-operative federalism?
Apparently winning was more important than honour. In his game the score is irrelevant. The rules, written or otherwise, are there to be broken. All that matters is the glitter of the trophy at the pinnacle of power. When Lawrence was elected mayor of Edmonton, some people thought they might be getting a polished apple for the West; sadly, all we got was Decore.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Hudecki (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: ROLE OF MEDICINE IN LAW ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, concern over the uncertain role of medicine in law enforcement is growing among many Canadian doctors. The focal point of their concern is that government intervention in the practice of medicine is increasing, and the time-honoured concept of doctor-patient confidentiality is in a state of serious erosion. Some of the questions doctors are now asking are: should a physician be required to use his or her clinical skills, or the information gathered, to enforce the laws of the land? To what extent should he or she be allowed to use professional discretion in determining the relevance of the knowledge so acquired?
Doctors generally agree that confidentiality is not for their benefit but for the patient's. If this confidentiality is destroyed, patients will be reluctant to communicate certain intimate facts, and physicians will stop keeping accurate records. The Canadian Medical Association is particularly concerned about pending CSIS legislation which will give an investigator special status, authorizing him to go into a physician's office and obtain information pertaining to matters under investigation. Physicians need to be reassured that access to medical records is a rare requirement in protecting the security of Canada, and that it is to be subjected to a rigorous process of control and review by Ministers of the Crown and the judiciary, along with a Security Intelligence Review Committee.

subsubtopic: EXERCISE OF POLITICAL RIGHTS BY EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, earlier today a number of students from the Canadian Labour College gathered on Parliament Hill to make a clear statement


that public sector workers should have their political freedom. Over 400,000 public employees across the country are denied their basic political rights. In a democracy the freedom of a citizen to take political action is considered to be a basic right. It should only be removed when persons have proven themselves to be unworthy of that right. In the case of public sector workers, it was removed because the political Parties, their employers, were abusing the power and the system.
In the 1980 federal election all political Parties were asked if they supported the principle that public sector workers should have the same basic rights as other citizens to participate in the political processes of Canada, and, if elected, would their Parties introduce legislation to that effect. All three Parties agreed that the law should be reviewed and revised. In 1979 an all-Party committee said:
Simply because political participation is a right of citizens, we believe that this should be the principle that applies to public servants, only limited in the exceptional cases where any indication of partisan political interests would compromise the reputation of the public service for impartiality or would damage the individual's effectiveness as a public servant.
Only the NDP has kept that promise. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), has at present just such a Bill on the Order Paper, C-248, and I ask all Members to help keep their own Parties-

subsubtopic: POLLUTION OF ONTARIO RIVERS-DELAY IN PAYMENT OF COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1970 the English and Wabigoon River systems in Ontario were declared unsafe due to methyl mercury pollution from the Reed Paper Company's pulp mill at Dryden. These rivers are still closed today. The closing of these rivers destroyed the economic base of two Indian communities. The Indians of White Dog and Grassy Narrows lost their incomes, their employment, their source of food, as well as their dignity. Since then Great Lakes Forest Products bought out the Reed Paper Company after that company agreed to compensate the native community with some SI5 million. To date this has not been done, after 15 years.
In the interest of human dignity and justice, I would urge the Prime Minister-elect to use his new position, and I might add his position as director of CP Limited and CP Investments, which are the major shareholders of Great Lakes Forest Products, to put in a good word and urge this company, of which he is still a small part, to fulfil their promise of compensation to the native population of Grassy Narrows and White Dog.

subsubtopic: URUGUAY-DETENTION OF OPPOSITION LEADER AND SON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I would like to bring to the attention of the House the fact that Amnesty International has declared that Wilson Ferreira and his son, Juan Raul Ferreira, are detained in custody in the country of Uruguay. This man was the Leader of the opposition Party which is known as the Blancos. He was attempting to return to Uruguay to participate in the election which is scheduled for October. During the 11 years that he has been in exile he has protested against the human rights violations which have taken place in his own country. Members of this House in all three Parties who served on the Latin American sub-committee know about this situation from personal experience. Ferreira has attempted to bring this reality to the whole world.
At this time I call upon the Government of Canada to protest vehemently against what has happened to Mr. Ferreira, a fellow parliamentarian, if it has not done so already. I call upon the Minister of External Affairs to ensure that our embassy in Buenos Aires, which looks after Uruguay, approaches the Government of that country to see that these two people are released immediately from prison.

Mr. Speaker, Canada Post Corporation has of late taken many interesting detours from its only mandate, delivering the mail. It has experimented with selling goods for Consumers Distributing, and has considered selling sports pool tickets. While on its detours it seems to have lost its sense of time and direction.
I received a complaint from a constituent this week which described how it took from May 18 until June 9, 22 days, to deliver a letter from Toronto to Bolsover, Ontario, a distance of 75 miles. Another constituent waited 13 days in May for a cheque to be delivered from Pefferlaw to Markham, a distance which can be travelled in less than an hour. Yet another constituent demanded a trailer be unloaded by Canada Post to see if it contained a christening gown which was long overdue. Sure enough, when the trailer was searched the gown was found, long after the christening.
On behalf of my constituents and all Canadians I urge the Government to allow Canada Post to return to its primary mandated function. It is about time it devoted its time to improving mail service and nothing else.

Mr. Speaker, as Hon. Members of the House will know, we have been engaged in developing a number of new initiatives in the area of airline policy designed to provide more choice for consumers. Member for Sarnia-Lambton was to point out that, on the question of adjustments that might be occasioned as a result of this, it would be a matter best left to the negotiations between management and labour. As the Minister to whom the CTC must answer, I am in the position where I may have to deal with an appeal or response, and therefore would not want to make any judgment at this time. That would be stepping beyond my bounds and would not allow the CTC to give full and proper account to the representations made before it. We are certainly taking into very deep and serious consideration that it is a matter of concern to the railways and the railway unions. The actions taken are to follow the normal prescribed procedures and not interfere or intervene in an unnatural way and simply distort the process.

POSSIBLE UNITED STATES ACTION TO CURTAIL STEEL IMPORTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Minister for International Trade regarding the ruling which was made by the International Trade Commission in the United States. That ruling was made under the safeguard of GATT. It could well affect some $700 million worth of Canadian steel exports to the United States. Could the Minister inform the House and the workers employed in that industry what action his Government has taken to protect that large amount of export, as well as the thousands of jobs which are in jeopardy as a result of the ruling by the International Trade Commission?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerald Regan (Minister for International Trade):
subtopic: POSSIBLE UNITED STATES ACTION TO CURTAIL STEEL IMPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would be happy to inform the Hon. Member of some of the things which we are doing. First, our opposition to such action by the United States has been made known by the
Deputy Prime Minister to Secretary of State Shultz. I have made it quite clear to the United States Secretary of Trade, Mr. Brock, on several occasions during the time that this investigation, under the petition, was proceeding. We are now in the process, both at the ministerial level and through the Canadian Embassy in Washington, of making it quite clear to the Americans that they have existing mechanisms for pinpointing the transgressors who may be creating the problem to the extent that it exists, and that they are not required to take this universal type of action.
What has happened thus far under their law is that a quasi-judicial investigation is under way which cannot be turned off by the U.S. Government. The American administration cannot stop the investigation. The only point at which the Government of the United States becomes involved is after July 24, when the USITC reports to the President. At that point our Government will deal with the American administration. Actually, we are dealing with them in advance. On Monday I am meeting with representatives from the Canadian steel industry to ensure that efforts are co-ordinated between industry and Government. I am also keeping the provinces informed.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):

speechtext:
1.
The proposed Customs and Excise Offshore Application Act was introduced as a Ways and Means Motion on December 7, 1983, retroactive to June 30, 1983. This motion provides for revisions to the Customs Tariff as it pertains to various types of vessels and other water-borne craft. In essence, provision is made for a 25 per cent rate of duty applicable to most vessels and other water-borne craft with the exception of drilling rigs and platforms which are rated at 20 per cent duty. The other main provisions of the motion are to expand tariff jurisdiction to British registered craft and to extend customs jurisdiction offshore to the greater of 200 miles and the edge of the continental shelf.
Recognizing that capital goods such as ships, drilling rigs and platforms are ordered considerably in advance of delivery date, the proposed legislation contains a provision exempting from duty any such goods ordered on or before January 6, 1983, which would otherwise have been subject to duty. January 6, 1983, was the date on which the Government announced publicly its intention to seek legislation in this area.

The House resumed consideration of Bill C-9, an Act to establish the Canadian Security Intelligence Service, to enact an Act respecting enforcement in relation to certain security and related offences and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof or in relation thereof, as reported (with amendments), from the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs; and Motions Nos. 75, 77 and 78 (Mr. Robinson (Burnaby), and Motion No. 79 (Mr. Fraser).

Mr. Speaker, a couple of minutes before nine last night I was addressing the House on several amendments, but in particular one which this
Security Intelligence Service
Party has put forward. I want to take this opportunity to say to my friend, the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan), that he is correct about one thing; there were several amendments accepted at committee. I thought I left the impression yesterday that there were no substantive amendments accepted. However, I have looked at the record and I am prepared to say, out of courtesy to my friend, that I should have stuck with the word "substantive", because there were several amendments accepted. However, I still remain of the opinion that the amendments accepted were not substantive amendments.
I also remind the Minister again that the amendment to Clause 39, which would have allowed the review committee to see the Cabinet documents that refer to the security service, which was passed in committee, is now being attacked by the Minister with a specific amendment wiping it out. I am honour bound to correct the record which I regret was not absolutely accurate but, as I say, my position in substance is sustained.
The provision we speak to now concerns Clause 31 of the Act. What is all that about? I know that today the media are watching this debate and they will be interested in this. Clause 31 follows Clause 30, of course, which sets out the functions of the Inspector General. Under this Bill the Inspector General is to:
(a)	to monitor the compliance by the Service with its operational policies;
(b)	to review the operational activities of the Service; and
(c)	to submit certificates pursuant to subsection 33(2).
The Inspector General is a review officer. He will make sure that this service conducts itself properly and within the mandate as set out in Bill C-9. What our amendment does is to say that the Inspector General should be able to see the Cabinet documents that relate to the activities of the intelligence gathering service. It is necessary to have such an amendment because the Solicitor General made sure that this Bill came in with a special provision that, notwithstanding the fact that the Inspector General was to do this review, he is not allowed to look at Cabinet documents. Exactly the same provision is in Clause 39, which I referred to, with respect to the review committee. It is not allowed to see the Cabinet documents related to the security service either. As I just reminded the Solicitor General, we got an amendment through committee, by accident, I suppose, because some Government Member did not vote, that would have allowed the review committee to see the Cabinet documents which relate to the security service. That is going to be wiped out by an amendment which the Government will get through in this place. This amendment deals specifically with allowing the Inspector General to see them. It is obvious why we ask that. In the words of the Senate committee report on the old Bill C-157, the Inspector General is to be "the Ministry's eyes and ears on the service". Clearly the Ministry's eyes and ears on the service should allow the Inspector General to see the Cabinet documents.


Security Intelligence Service
The Senate committee also said:
If any Cabinet documents relating to operations are in the control of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service, the Inspector General should have access to them.
It is very curious that the Solicitor General cites the Senate committee report for what he chooses to put in the Bill and ignores it for what he chooses not to put in the Bill. In a speech the Attorney General of Ontario gave in Ottawa on February 7, 1984 he said:
The danger is that this secrecy provision can permit the Government to exercise political control over the activities of the service in a manner which is immune from effective review. I believe that there is great merit in the words of Professor Peter Russel, who said in relation to the denial of access to Cabinet documents that: "A Government that is itself so distrustful is not entitled to the trust that this legislation demands from the people it represents."
To make it absolutely clear once again today why we are so angry in this Chamber, it is that these are the kind of substantive amendments which were put forward in committee after listening for weeks to eminent Canadians who appeared before the committee and said that there are things we should do to fix that Bill up. These are the substantive amendments that the Solicitor General and the Government, now headed by the reform man, John Turner, is absolutely refusing to accept. That is the charade and shame that is going on in this Chamber.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of the motions which are presently before the House. These motions deal with two very important clauses in the Bill. I do not think I would argue that they are the most essential clauses by any stretch of the imagination. Yet the Minister has argued strongly that the Inspector General, who is appointed pursuant to the provisions of these two clauses which are before the House now, is indeed to be the Minister's man, an independent watchdog, within the frame work of the security service.
Let us look at the motions which we are dealing with. The motions would delete Clauses 30 and 31 and would ensure that if Clause 31 is passed the Inspector General should have access to all documents in the possession of the security service. That is a fundamental principle which I would hope Members of the House would see fit to adopt.
With respect to the role of the Inspector General, I argued strongly in committee that this position should only be filled following consultation with and ratification by members of all Parties in the House. It is not good enough that the Government should be in the position of appointing the person who is effectively supposed to act as the watchdog, on a day to day basis, of the operations of the proposed civilian security service. There should be consultations which extend beyond the Government merely talking to itself.
The most important element of the amendments which are being dealt with in this package of amendments is Motion No. 78. That motion would delete the glaring loophole which now exists in this Bill which denies the Inspector General, the person who is supposed to have day to day surveillance of the
activities of the new service, access to what are called confidences of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada. The Solicitor General introduced Bill C-157 last May which was supposedly the Government's best response to the recommendations of the McDonald Commission. That Bill was soundly condemned from one end of the country to the other by every analyst and group that read it. Despite that, the same Minister was parading up and down the country telling us what a tremendous Bill it was and what an improvement it was in terms of the protection of civil liberties of Canadians. The same Minister, having suggested that the predecessor Bill, Bill C-157, was a wonderful Bill and a work of art, now comes before the House and asks us to trust him again. Some of us have some difficulties in doing that.
The Pitfield committee, which was chaired by Senator Pit-field in the other place, made a series of recommendations for improving Bill C-15. A unanimous recommendation made by that committee was that if the watchdog was to have any power whatsoever he should obviously have access to documents in the possession of the security service. It sounds pretty straight-forward. If the watchdog, appointed to ensure that there are no political abuses of the operations of a new civilian security service, went to the Director of the service and said that he understood there had been a directive received from the Solicitor General instructing him to spy on the peace movement and asking to see that directive-
All directives of the minister are available.
-which falls within the definition of a confidence of the Queen's Privy Council-
It does not. If it is a directive it does not.
That document falls within the definition of the confidence of the Queen's Privy Council. That is an incredibly broad definition.
It certainly does not include directives to the service.

I will welcome the Solicitor General's intervention on this point in defence of his rejection of the recommendation by the Pitfield committee on this important amendment. If that is the case, the Director of the new civilian security service can tell the so-called watchdog to get lost. He can say that he does not have to show him that document.
The Committee on Security and Intelligence, which is chaired by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and of which the Solicitor General is a member, decides the mandate and scope of the Communications Security Establishment. That is the shadowy body which has the power and technical capacity to spy on literally any conversation in the country. The Solicitor General asks us to trust them because the Cabinet does not allow them to do that under its present mandate. What if another Cabinet, at the stroke of a pen, as they could do, changed the mandate of the Communications Security Establishment? They could say that henceforth the CSE will be


used to feed information to the civilian security service. We are put in a ludicrous position under the terms of this Bill. If the Inspector General somehow got wind of that particular decision and demanded to see the documents in question from the Director of the security service, the Director could tell the Inspector General that he does not have to show him that document. So much for the confidence of the Canadian people in the oversight process of this particular civilian security service.
I emphasize that Senator Pitfield is not a person who lightly recommends that certain confidences of the Queen's Privy Council be made accessible to any individual. Indeed, he was the chief architect of the exemption in the access to information law that led to that particular exemption. Yet that same individual along with other members of the Senate committee said that if there is to be effective oversight and if the public of this country is to have confidence in the oversight mechanism, surely as a minimum, if these documents are already in the possession of the security service, they should not be denied to the people who are supposed to be scrutinizing the activities of that same service. That was the recommendation of the Pit-field committee which the Minister chose to ignore.
I am pleased to say that at least one member on the Government side who I see in the House today, the Hon. Member for Rosemont (Mr. Lachance), who was chairman of the committee, strongly urged the committee to accept it. However, despite those urgings by that member of the committee and by a former Solicitor General, the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), what does the Government do? It says to forget it; it will not trust its own appointed watchdogs with those documents. What incredible arrogance! What a devastating blow to the oversight process that the Government is suggesting meets the concerns of the public in terms of accountability!
The Government denies the right of Parliament to play a role. The basis for its rejection of Parliament's role is that there is another oversight process, an Inspector General and a review committee. That oversight process is gutted of any effective strengths if the Government defeats the motion which is before the House at this point. I appeal to Members of the House to look at what they are doing in terms of the future of this country, to look at what they are doing in terms of oversight. Surely it is not an unreasonable proposition that this motion, which would ensure that the watchers are able to fully carry out their mandate of scrutiny, must be adopted if that mandate is to be pursued with any effectiveness at all.

Mr. Speaker, I also wish to make a few comments on this clause. Having spent several days listening to the clause by clause debate and to the amendments that have been proposed, you can see that this Bill is defective in many ways. However, it is not so defective that it could not be improved if we had more time to do so. The only reason we are being forced on this long march
Security Intelligence Service
is that the Minister is worried about the end of the session approaching and he wants to have this Bill go through.
We have heard about the defects to the Bill and listened to arguments about whether the service should remain with the RCMP or should be a new civilian agency. It is an honest difference of view and while I believe it should remain with the RCMP, as do 75 per cent of the people, more time would let people hear the arguments on both sides and resolve it. It is evident that in this great country of ours it takes a month before people on the street really do come to see the issues clearly.
Do you think it has been a month? It has been 18.

It has not been before the House of Commons for that long. When we are debating it in the House, that is when it really does get into the homes of the people.
We have also heard the dispute over the powers. We believe that the agency has too many powers. As parliamentarians, we should let the agency begin with narrow powers and expand them in the future if needed.
We have heard arguments on judicial warrants. We have also introduced amendments to limit the time of their effectiveness. Unfortunately, the Government has rejected all of these very reasonable amendments that would perfect the Bill rather than leave it in its present defective state.
With respect to Clause 30 which deals with the Inspector General, while it is a good idea to have oversight on a day-to-day basis by a person who is responsible to the Minister, the credibility of that man or woman could be vastly improved if there was consultation on the appointment of that person so that it was seen to be a position like that of the Auditor General who is accountable to Parliament rather than to the Minister himself. Perhaps that is an idea worth considering. The Minister refused to consider these ideas. We also believe that that individual should be able to see the same documents on which decisions are being made in order properly to enforce his or her mandate and be able to hear both sides of the story. Yet the Minister is restricting that person from seeing these documents, which are Cabinet documents.
As the Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) told us in committee, the Cabinet documents which may be involved have been accessible not only by the Minister but the executive assistant to the Minister and the secretaries who typed the document. In fact, several layers of the bureaucracy have access to Cabinet documents and they are not nearly as secret as we might believe. As the former Solicitor General asked, why are we restricting that document from the Inspector General, who is supposed to be a check, when several layers of the bureaucracy at the political level and in the civil service have had access to it?
The Minister's arguments to restrict Cabinet documents failed on the weight of the evidence. I hope that even at this late stage Government Members will remind the Minister that he has been generous in the past. I agree that the Government


Security Intelligence Service
has been generous in opening up the process for public scrutiny and it deserves credit for that. This would be a further step in that direction and would bring great honour to the Minister. Therefore I would ask him once again to change his mind and give the Inspector General at least access to these Cabinet documents.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bob Kaplan (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I should take a moment to explain once again the Government's position with respect to confidences of the Queen's Privy Council. I know that I cannot make any yards with the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson). He challenged the Government to be reasonable. He is a Member who does not know the meaning of the word reasonable. If he did, I think we would have had more legislation proceed through this Parliament. In fact, in the context of this amendment, it makes me think of the great difficulty that the NDP has in recognizing the necessity to balance a variety of interests in order to get anywhere. They take the attitude, particularly the Member for Burnaby, that in measure after measure if they cannot get the whole cake, all the icing and all the candles, they would rather starve.
That is not the kind of attitude that permits any Parliament to work. In this particular case, Bill C-157, which I think is greatly improved by Bill C-9, was in itself a considerable improvement over the present arrangements. Bill C-9 takes us that much further. If the Hon. Member had his way and this Bill did not proceed, we would have no reform at all to the system of national security. The Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) was good enough to recognize that the review process, which is a reform in itself, does represent a considerable improvement and step forward. But as far as the Hon. Member for Burnaby is concerned, unless he gets his amendments or all the amendments, the review process is meaningless.
Let me suggest that the review process as it appears in the Bill is very meaningful. I appreciate the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills recognizing that it is in itself a step forward. The Inspector General and the review committee open the door. Although I can never explain adequately to the Member for Burnaby, let me explain again why it is that confidences of the Queen's Privy Council will-

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The Minister continues to make reference to the need to explain to the Member for Burnaby. The Minister has to explain to the people of this country why he is mandating a service without proper overview.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. If the Hon. Member wants to rise on a point of order, he should stick to a point of order. That is debate.

During the administration of the Prime Minister, this Government has moved very considerably to reduce all of the prerogatives of the Government and of the Queen's Privy Council. I would say, and I do not think anyone here could contradict me, that the prerogatives of government have
been reduced by legislation more in the last 16 years than in any comparable period in the history of the parliamentary system of government. We have introduced access to information legislation so that the former prerogative of the Government to keep all documents confidential unless it chooses otherwise has been very considerably reduced. We have introduced the Canada Evidence Act amendments which have reduced the number of documents that can be withheld from court process. We have introduced the Crown Liability Act so that the prerogative could not be asserted which prevented citizens of this country from using the Crown as a matter of right. That power has been reduced. In so many ways we have moved to reduce prerogatives of the Crown, and we have done it for a very good reason. It is because we want, to the maximum extent possible, to have an open and accessible government.
This is not recognized at all by the New Democratic Party but I know it is recognized by the Canadian people. One very important reservation which continues to be reserved are confidences of the Queen's Privy Council. These have been reserved in the Canada Evidence Act. These have been reserved in the Access to Information Act, and they have been reserved for the very good reason that in the opinion of this Government the functioning Cabinet, under the cabinet system of government, requires that Ministers of the Crown and their advisers can communicate with each other in confidence. We think that government is more effective, that decisions are better, if members of the government and their advisers can communicate with each other knowing that those exchanges will not be made public and will not be made available beyond the realm of the cabinet system without the approval of the Prime Minister.
I do not know, but Hon. Members opposite in the New Democratic Party have never given any weight at all to this requirement of cabinet government. I am wasting my time to ask them to do so. I would like, at least for the benefit of the people in the gallery, to explain that you cannot have as effective a cabinet system of government if confidences are not protected.
Tell that to Michael Pitfield.

Let me explain that one of the aspects of privileged communication is advice. I go to Cabinet, and I take to my Cabinet colleagues the best advice I can about how things in the area of national security should be handled. That advice is what we are trying to protect here. If that advice has to be made public or can ultimately be made public, or it is accessible to anyone, there is a very good chance that the Minister will not ask for advice because he may decide not to take it. If he knows that advice can be made public and he can be asked to explain why he asked for advice, why good advice was given to him and he did not take it, he will be less inclined to get advice. The same thing applies to legal advice. I have encouraged all of my officials to get legal advice from the law officers of the Crown whenever they think it will be helpful to


them. That advice is privileged. If they knew that advice could be made public whenever somebody requested it, they would be less inclined to seek advice. I think it is in the interest of good government in this country that that advice should be sought. We are seeking to reserve the prerogative of confidence of the Queen's Privy Council, notwithstanding the establishment of this review committee.
The Hon. Member opposite says that if they cannot get Queen's Privy Council confidences, the whole review process is useless. How wrong that is. I can tell the Hon. Member opposite that no privileges of the Queen's Privy Council have gone to the security service in all of the time that I have been Solicitor General. If that privilege were removed, there would be nothing to be made public under that heading so far as decisions or discussions of Cabinet Ministers going to the security service are concerned.
I think again Hon. Members opposite are very seriously exaggerating the significance of Queen's Privy Council confidences so far as the operations of the new agency are concerned. I can assure them that the review committee system and the Inspector General system will be very effective without it.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to make a few comments on the little sermon we just heard from the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan). First, the Solicitor General is dead wrong and he knows that he is dead wrong when he says, as he just did, and as he said on other occasions, that members of the New Democratic Party will not support a proposal, not support legislation, unless it contains everything they want. Nothing could be further from the truth, Mr. Speaker.
I can think of two matters which are still before the House about which we are very co-operative in order to get them through before Parliament adjourns, even though they do not meet the problems which we think they are supposed to solve. We are not satisfied with the proposal to increase the guaranteed income supplement by $50 a month, but we will support it because it is better than nothing at all. We are not satisfied with the amendments to the Labour Code which are being brought forward. We think much more should have been done. In as far as they go, they are an improvement on what we have had. We not only support them but we have indicated very clearly that we will let them through with very little debate on our part.
Those are just two illustrations of the policy we have always followed of supporting legislation if it moves in the right direction, even though it does not contain anything we want.
I think the Solicitor General almost dislocated his shoulder trying to pat himself on the back while speaking. He talked about how Parliament had become more relevant and how much more open the Government is than it used to be. There is a consensus in the country and, I am sure, among Members of Parliament who do not happen to be Cabinet Ministers-I speak not just of Members of the Opposition but of backbench Members on the Government side-that Parliament has
Security Intelligence Service
never been as irrelevant, has never been as little consulted, because the Government decides everything in advance and simply will not listen to any suggestions no matter from where they come.
The Minister talked about the great Access to Information Act. I have had some experience with that Act. We know from the McDonald Commission report that the RCMP security service collected personal files on 700,000 Canadians. I had a suspicion that I may have been one of those people. I followed all the procedures, filled out all the forms, and applied for permission to see my file. I still do not know whether the RCMP has a file on me, although I am reasonably certain it does because I was told that under the provisions of the Access to Information Act such information is confidential. Therefore, I cannot be told even whether there is or not.
Similarly, and I have mentioned this already, using the United States Freedom of Information Act, I applied for the same kind of information from the Federal Bureau of Investigation. Lo and behold, not being a citizen of the United States, I got from the Federal Bureau of Investigation what they had on me in their files. It was not of any consequence, but there is the difference. That is just one single illustration of the difference between the American Act and the Canadian Act. Our Act is to a large extent a hoax, just another way of creating the image that the Government has done something when in fact it has done very little.
It is the same thing with this Bill, Mr. Speaker. Of course, we need an Act with regard to the security service. What was wrong before was that there was little or no control over the security service. We do not need an Act which purports to lay down rules, regulations and procedures that the security service shall follow and at the same time gives it the power to do, not only everything it wants to do, but that which it did before that the McDonald Commission, among others, indicated was improper and immoral and broke the law. This Bill is changing the law to give the security service the right to do the things which it was not permitted legally to do before.
The Solicitor General, either deliberately or because he does not understand, tried to suggest that we are proposing in this amendment that all Cabinet documents be made available to the public. This is not the time nor the place to discuss what Cabinet documents should be made public. However, it is interesting to anyone who follows what happens in the United States to look at some of the books and articles published in recent years in that country. They will see the vast amount of information about what is going on in the American Government which is now available to the public-Cabinet documents, remarks of Secretaries, who are comparable with our Ministers, and so on.
What we are saying in this proposal is that the Inspector General is supposed to be the watchdog. Supposedly he is the person who will guarantee to the public that the security service is not misusing its powers. The Inspector General is to be the watchdog. The public is to assume that he is there and
4880


Security Intelligence Service
has the authority to ensure that the security service does not overstep its bounds, does not break the law, and gives adequate protection to the people of Canada. If the Inspector General cannot be trusted to get all relevant information, to see all relevant documents and to see all the motions passed by Cabinet, what is the point of having an Inspector General? The only point is the one that we have come to expect from Liberal governments. They will give the appearance of doing something and of dealing with a question. They will create the appearance that the public is being protected while in fact they, the security service or any other department, will be able to continue in the same secretive, high-handed, unilateral manner in terms of decision-making as they always have. This is why we proposed this amendment and why the Solicitor General ought not to try to cloud the issue.

office during good behaviour for a term not exceeding seven years." and by renumbering subsection (4) accordingly.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of these motions which are now before the House, Motions Nos. 85 and 86, is to attempt to point out some very serious deficiencies in the proposed wording of the legislation with respect to the socalled watchdog, the Security Intelligence Review Committee or the SIRC, as it is known.
The Government does not trust Members of Parliament to oversee the operations of the new service. It refused to accept the recommendation of the McDonald Commission in this respect. It refused to accept the precedents of West Germany, United States and a number of other countries in this respect. Instead the Government says that we should trust its oversight process because it is establishing the Security Intelligence Review Committee.
What are some of the flaws in that oversight process, that SIRC process? First, although there is a requirement for consultation before the appointment of the members of that review committee, ultimately it is a decision of the Government as to who will be named to the committee. Government Members can name cronies of the Liberal Government or whomever else they choose without any opportunity for Members of the Opposition to have an effective say in the choice of members of the review committee. In terms of the appointment process, that is the first flaw in this provision.
Second, having appointed these people, what powers do they have under the terms of the legislation? The first constraint on the review committee is that it is bound by an oath of secrecy. Members of the review committee are bound by an oath of secrecy, so they cannot report to Parliament, to the elected representatives of the people of the country, anything which would breach their oath of secrecy. What kind of effective oversight does that give to Parliament? This secret, shadowy security service will be operating without any meaningful accountability whatsoever.
Another significant barrier to effective oversight is the fact that the review committee will not have the power, if the amendment proposed by the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) is accepted in due course, to access Cabinet documents or confidences of the Queen's Privy Council.
I could do no better than quote Professor Peter Russell who talked about the sheer arrogance of this provision and how ridiculous it was that one group of Privy Councillors was not prepared to trust another group of Privy Councillors with information already in the hands of the security service. That effectively guts the review process of any meaning or any substance whatsoever.
Let us look at the tremendous powers which the new security service will have. It will have the power to break into anyone's home, to break into an office or any other place, to steal documents, to remove literally anything it wants to remove, to have access to confidential medical and psychiatric records, to have access to journalists' documents, the offices of Members of Parliament and their documents, and to have access to income tax records. The list goes on and on. We are told not to worry because there will be an oversight committee which will ensure that there are no abuses.


1 suggest that this oversight committee is a completely toothless watchdog because it does not even have access to the essential documents in the hands of the security service. Some of us suspected that the RCMP security service was hung out to dry because of the failure on the part of former Solicitors General to accept political responsibility for their actions. That would continue to be possible under the provisions of this legislation.
We say that the oversight process is a sham. Only the involvement of Members of Parliament in a parliamentary oversight committee, as was strongly recommended by the McDonald Commission, is adequate if these sweeping new powers are not to become a political weapon in the hands of the government of the day. That is the purpose of Motion No. 85, to delete Clause 34.
Motion No. 86 would change the length of tenure of the proposed review committee from one term of five years which would be renewable for a second five-year term to one nonrenewable term of five years. There is a real danger that the agency which is established to oversee the operations of the new security service could become captured by the very service that it is supposed to be overseeing.
There is a danger that if members of the review committee are currying favour with the Government and seeking reappointment to their positions, they will not be as vigilant in their oversight. Limited though it may be, they will not be as vigilant in that oversight as they should be. The amendment before the House would establish a term of office of seven years and would provide that that term should not be renewed in order to prevent that kind of toadying to the government of the day by the review committee.
The bottom line in this series of motions now before the House is that the Government has betrayed the trust of the people it was elected to represent. It refuses to provide for meaningful accountability and oversight for the operations of this new service which theoretically would have the power to say no, no to the suggestion that the security service might target hundreds of thousands of Canadians. Indeed, the RCMP security service opened files on close to one million Canadians, men and women who broke no law whatsoever, activists in the peace movement, activitists in support of the liberation movements in South America and South Africa; yet this Government has the audacity to bring a Bill before this House that would in effect countenance and make legal what was so clearly documented as being illegal by the McDonald Commission, institutionalized wrongdoing.
The purpose of these motions is very fundamental. It is no less than an attempt to restore some semblance of parliamentary oversight; failing that, it is an attempt to ensure that this toothless watchdog, the review committee which is denied access to documents in the possession of the security service, should at the very least not be currying favour with the government of the day in an attempt to win reappointment. Surely this Parliament should accept nothing less if we are
Security Intelligence Service
serious about any kind of oversight of the operations of such a powerful agency in a democratic society.

Mr. Speaker, Clause 34 which sets up the Security Intelligence Review Committee is another area where our Party differs substantially from the Government. Canadians are entitled to be aware of the difference. Our view is that the officials of the review committee, SIRC, should be elected. Our neighbour to the South with its enormous security problems has its CIA and FBI accountable to an elected body of officials both in the Senate and in the House of Representatives. It is the elected officials who bear the ultimate responsibility to the people. We find that principle attractive.
Canadians need to know that the Government is not of the view that it should be putting responsibility and trust in the elected officials, that it wants to leave those responsibilities with people that it, the Cabinet, appoints. It is always dangerous to put information into the hands of elected people who are accountable to the populace in general. They may act in the interest of the people instead of in the interest of the government of the day. As we know from the actions of the Liberal Government, it finds that to be dangerous. People need to know. We have that fundamental difference as to who would be on this body.
When you look at the appointees to the hundreds of Crown corporations who have been appointed by the Governor in Council, the Cabinet, you see immediately why we are concerned. While a Crown corporation can work in certain jurisdictions, whenever they got into deep trouble it has been as a result of the appointees to their boards, appointed by the Liberal patronage machine. Canadair lost almost $2 billion of taxpayers' money, yet the directors of Canadair, all appointed by the Liberal Cabinet, received an increase in salary this year. They are not truly responsible because they are just political hacks rather than people who are genuinely accountable to the shareholders of that corporation, de Havilland also lost money. Every few years this Parliament has to write off $700 million or $800 million which CNR has lost because its directors, appointed through the political patronage of the Liberal Party, have not done their job. When Canadians see the billions of dollars that Petro-Canada has lost with the senior management of that corporation having been appointed by the Liberal patronage machine, they will be absolutely ill. They will be sick at heart because the Government does not have to operate that way. The Government will have to live with the judgment of the people in the next election.
In trying to ease the concern of people, the Government said that appointments would only be made after consultation with the Leader of the Opposition in the House of Commons and the Leader in the House of Commons of each Party having at least 12 members. That is a small step. I suppose consultation is better than absolutely nothing. However, let us look at what the witnesses said. These people tried to do what was right. They took time to read the Bill, ponder it, discuss it, and then gave us the benefit of their thinking. For example, the CJC suggested that in naming its members, the Prime Minister


Security Intelligence Service
should seek the consent of the Leader of the Opposition and should consult the Leaders of the other Parties in the House.
I would go further. If we really want SIRC to have genuine credibility, the Leader of the Official Opposition should be able to appoint one in three or three in five of the review committee. The purpose of the review committee is to lend credibility to the security service so that Canadians know that that security service is not getting into areas that it should not. If we want that committee, which will have to issue a report to Parliament, to be totally believable, the ideal situation would be to have a key person involved, and it should be the Leader of Her Majesty's Official Opposition. If that person were to appoint one out of three or two out of five of the commissioners, the Government would still do the bulk of the appointing but the committee would have enormous credibility if the Leader of the Official Opposition had that right.
Again the Government rejected that proposal, which we had put forward sincerely. The witnesses thought that there should be opposition consent, if not outright opposition appointment, and the Government rejected that. Therefore, as is true with all of the other proposals, whether they are to leave the service with the RCMP, the power of the agency is too broad or the judicial warrants are in effect for too long a period of time, the Government will have to accept the judgment of the Canadian people. The Canadian peole will have to take this matter in hand to get their sovereignty back. The Government will have to be defeated so that a new Government can continue an ongoing review process and make changes to bring the legislation back into line with our traditional Canadian freedoms which we have all come to respect and which I believe are being pushed rather hard by this Bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap).

Mr. Speaker, this grouping of motions concerns the clause by which the members of the review committee are appointed. It has been pointed out that the chief problem with the manner of appointment is that this review committee becomes the creature of the Government. Its members are appointed by the Government only, perhaps with some little official consultation. The appointments are decided on only by the Government and the appointees are therefore not in any sense responsible to Parliament.
It is not surprising that the Government, after indicating that the group will not be appointed by Parliament or be in any sense responsible to Parliament, has further indicated that the group should not trust Parliament and must take an oath of secrecy which separates it from Parliament. That oath would in fact bind the committee to the very group it is supposed to be watch-dogging. It is a strange kind of watchdog
which must have a greater loyalty to the group it is supposed to watch than to the group whose interests it is supposed to defend. That is the case here.
This committee will owe its first obligation to the Minister's secret service and any obligation to Parliament will only be such that the secret service will allow. That is to say, the secret service will tell this committee what its limits are under the oath of secrecy, what information it is permitted to reveal to Parliament and what information it is not permitted to reveal to Parliament. It is because of that that we are experiencing this charade of Privy Council confidences.
The Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) has said that there are no confidential Privy Council documents being used by the secret service at present. He did not say that no such documents would be used but he did say that there are not any being used at present and that this is not an issue. If in fact this is not an issue, he should not have insisted on putting that restriction into law. He contradicts himself in that way. What is he afraid of? Is he afraid that people who have been handpicked by the Government are not to be trusted? He tells us a ridiculous story about how every Cabinet document cannot be made public.
No one on this side of the House has suggested that every Cabinet document should be made public. We have suggested that if a Cabinet document has been made public to the extent of being shown to the security service for its use, something which the Minister says has not yet happened but clearly thinks might happen-and he might even want it to happen- then it should also be made available to one more person. It should not be made available to the whole world. It should not be made available to the press of Members of Parliament per se. It should be made available to the Inspector General and to the people who have already been hand-picked by the Government to review such documents. The Solicitor General acts in such a schizophrenic way that he now says that the group he is supposed to trust is not to be trusted.
The question is why we should trust the Solicitor General and the Government he represents. This is the party which used the War Measures Act against the Japanese in Canada 40 years ago, an action that has been regarded almost universally as being shameful and unjustified on the grounds then given of security. In recent years it has become apparent that the then Prime Minister and his Cabinet knew that such action was not justified on grounds of security because their own security advisers in the RCMP and the army had told them that it was not justified. They did it for other meaner purposes than security but used security as a cloak.
Likewise, the invasion of Montreal 14 years ago by the troops of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) occurred after the Liberal Government again invoked the War Measures Act for reasons that have not yet become clear. The actions taken at that time did help to disrupt a reform threat in the Montreal municipal elections but we really do not know what the Government was after. It certainly did not accomplish any of its stated purposes by invading Montreal with tanks and by


throwing 300 or 400 people into jail, none of whom was found chargeable.
Very soon the voters will be asked to elect Members of Parliament. They will be told by the smooth talkers in the Government that the people they elect will defend their liberties as well as do other good things. They will be told that they are sending people to Parliament to guide and if necessary oversee the Government. Yet if this Bill has been passed by that time, that purpose will be completely frustrated because those who will be sent to Parliament, even the majority of those on the government side, will not have an opportunity to look into what is happening with the security service. Only a privileged few within the Cabinet itself and perhaps a few other Privy councillors who are satisfactory to the Prime Minister will have that opportunity. No one elected to represent the great majority of the ridings in Canada will have any right to watch over the actions of the security service. That is a destruction of the liberties we enjoy in this country.
I received a telegram from one of my constituents which reads:
The Canadian Government sometimes forgets it is elected to serve the Canadian people. We, the Canadian public, cannot allow our fundamental rights to be "subverted" by government bureaucrats and the RCMP.
He might well have added to that "and by the new security service". This legislation will be marked as being the achievement of 1984 in Canada. The tradition of democratic control of the police, democratic control of the state that uses force and information search and intrusion techniques, democratic control of the powers of coercion, will be decisively taken away from the elected representatives of the country. That will be a sad day, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to delay the House but I do wish to say a word or two in regard to the Security Intelligence Review Committee. I think the provision for this committee is probably one of the most important items in the Bill because the public will depend upon the committee to see that things are done properly and correctly.
I would like to hear the comments of the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) on one or two points in connection with Clause 34. The committee is appointed by the Governor in Council or by Cabinet. The committee is therefore responsible to Cabinet, not to the House of Commons or to Parliament. I do not have any great objection to that, although I would much rather have it responsible to the Parliament of Canada. However, being responsible to the Cabinet is certainly not too farfetched if the Cabinet is responsible to the House of Commons and gives the House of Commons the information which is available and which it needs or wants.
There is a provision in Clause 6(2) which bothers me. That is the fact that the review committee is not able to give any information to the House of Commons committee for review. The House of Commons committee is denied that under Clause 6(3). It reads:
Security Intelligence Service
Directions issued by the Minister under subsection (2) shall be deemed not to be statutory instruments for the purposes of the Statutory Instruments Act.
Therefore, directions which are issued by the Minister to the review committee are being denied to the House of Commons committee. What is that? The committee in the House of Commons is composed of Members of Parliament from all Parties. The committee is the only access which Members of Parliament have to this type of information. If the House of Commons committee is denied information by a direction from the Minister and that information is made available to the Director or to the review committee, then that information is not available to Members of Parliament.
That is a very strange way of making Parliament responsible. Surely a committee set up in this House to review statutory instruments should have access to information which pertains to that. Why should information which concerns the civil liberties of the people of Canada be denied to a parliamentary committee? I cannot follow that. Is it that the parliamentary committee cannot be trusted? The review committee is being trusted. If it originally came from the Minister, that would mean that a number of public servants had already seen the information. Anyone in the Minister's office would have had access to that information. Several layers of public servants would have had access to it. Yet the House of Commons committee, which is set up by Parliament and under the rules of the House, would not be able to look at the information.
I do not think that is sound. If Parliament is responsible then the committee is accountable to Parliament and Parliament must have all of the facts-not just the facts which the review committee wants to give to it, but all of the facts. If the Parliament of Canada is denied that, it would indicate that the Parliament of Canada cannot be trusted; or, in broader terms, that the people of Canada cannot be trusted. The information should be made available to a committee of the House of Commons in order that it can analyse the information to determine if the information is right and proper. It might well be that a Minister issues directions which he feels are in good sense and good order. However, sometimes there are differences of views in regard to what is right and what is wrong. The Minister may very well issue instructions to a committee or to a public servant that are not correct and not in the interests of the people of Canada. Perhaps the instructions might be in the interests of an individual or in the interests of a political Party. Then what happens? A committee is set up in Parliament to review those instructions and to keep tab on them, but that committee cannot see them.
That is not accountability in my view. That is hiding the facts from the public. It is slipped in here in such an innocent way that I would think probably one out of every ten people would not even realize that it is in the legislation. Does the press realize that this type of information will not be given to the House of Commons committee which was set up to study it? I have not seen any mention of it in the newspapers. Therefore, the people outside this House are not able to receive the information. We might send a few of these Bills out to our


Security Intelligence Service
constituents. However, unless those constituents have been given some guidance as to what is going on and what parliamentary terms mean, the Bills become almost meaningless.
I would like to mention another point which has been raised by the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson). It is in connection with the oath of secrecy. When the members of the committee are appointed by the Government in Council, they must take an oath. That oath is included in the Bill. I have no objection whatsoever to the oath of office because I think it is right. I think there are bounds within which people who are members of committees must be restrained from giving information to every Tom, Dick and Harry or Mary, Ann and Josephine. However, surely that should not be applicable to Members of Parliament who are responsible to the people. The oath of secrecy reads:
I,. .. , swear that I will not, without due authority, disclose or make known to any person any information acquired by me by reason of the duties performed by me on behalf of or under the direction of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service or by reason of any office or employment held by me pursuant to the Canadian Security Intelligence Service Act. So help me God.
"Without due authority". From whom would they get the authority? From the Cabinet? Perhaps from the Minister. Normally the authority would be given by those who appoint a person. They are the only people who should have responsibility. When it is everybody's responsibility, it is nobody's responsibility.
I think we should give careful thought to this whole matter to ensure that this body will be responsible and accountable to Parliament-not only to the Cabinet but to Parliament which represents the people of Canada. That is the number one issue as far as I am concerned.

Mr. Speaker, this series of amendments is absolutely critical to the Bill, and Canadians genuinely have to understand that the Parties have a very distinct and different view of them. What the Government has done, I feel, is just simply wrong. It is going to pay a bitter penalty for it. While we think we could have convinced Government Members to make some changes, part of the problem is the New Democratic Party. It has attacked every clause with equal vehemence because it had no sense of judgment as to what was absolutely critical to the Bill, and because it has used an elephant gun even on the pigeons, now that we have come to an elephant. Because of its stalling tactics, Canadians do not appreciate how critical this clause is.
Let us not forget, Mr. Speaker, that the review committee, in our view, should have access to Cabinet documents. The Senate committee which looked at this matter and heard dozens of witnesses felt that the review committee should have access to Cabinet documents. The Government did not and so there was no access put into Bill C-9. The witnesses who came before the committee said that the review committee should have access to Cabinet documents. A motion was put forth to bring that about at committee stage and it was passed by that committee so that, as the Bill which was reported from the committee stood, the review committee would have access to Cabinet documents.
The Cabinet has now put forth Motion No. 96 which would reinstate secrecy and the review committee would not have access to Cabinet documents. I sat in committee that night when this clause was being discussed at committee stage. Government Members on the committee were divided. As a result, one of the Government Members voted for our amendment, and that was quite appropriate, Mr. Speaker.
I guess what I am saying is that we have a process here in Parliament and we should trust that process and not let a Cabinet lay on its heavy hand. The Government is wrong. The Government is abusing the parliamentary process with the amendment it has put forth. It is abusing the trust of the Canadian people. Those Government Members are going to have to be defeated, every single one of them in the next
Security Intelligence Service
election, by the looks of it, in order that we can get that trust back.
On this question, Mr. Speaker, I urge the Liberal backbenchers to search their conscience and to look at this issue. We know many of those Hon. Members believe there should be access to Cabinet documents. Indeed, the former Solicitor General who was part of the Cabinet and was the Solicitor General through the FLQ crisis, or at least part of that time, believes that this review committee must have access to Cabinet documents in order for that review committee to have credibility for it to be able to function effectively in holding the agency to account.
Where is Mr. Turner on this issue, Mr. Speaker? We know that his first official act in his role as pro tern Prime Minister, after being briefed in the afternoon, was to permit closure to be brought in on this Bill. We know that his second act was to have this Bill attack the real cultural tradition of this institution.

speechtext: How do you know that?

I presume that the Liberals are smart enough to brief their pro tem Prime Minister. Am I to assume, Mr. Speaker, that those Hon. Members are not informing their leader of these attacks on our institution?
However, his third act, Mr. Speaker, is to condone an action whereby the Cabinet is attacking the very parliamentary process which he claims he is going to strengthen. He is calling for more free votes. Well, let us have a free vote on this because I am confident that the Liberal Members of Parliament, in using their heads, would agree with our position on the issue and would vote with us. Indeed, they did at the committee stage, Mr. Speaker. Now Cabinet is going to sit on its members. Cabinet is saying to those Hon. Members: "You might be elected by the people, but if you do not go with us, we are going to hurt you. You will not get on any boards or commissions. There will be no judicial appointments for you. Either you fall in line or we will punish you". That is how the Liberal Cabinet has traditionally kept those Hon. Members in line.
Motion No. 94 in the name of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser), should also be accepted, and I believe it would be accepted by Liberal back-benchers if we could have a free vote. What this motion says is that the review committee should not only have access to the documents and the work of the security service, but it should also have access to the security functions of other branches of government.
For example, we know that the External Affairs Department conducts extensive intelligence work, as does the Department of National Defence. Yet only the new agency will be subjected to overview by this review committee. Given the history of this Cabinet, there is no doubt what it will do when it is into something it wants to be kept secret. It will try to get the security service to do it. If the Director, because he has a review committee, says no, he will not touch that with a


Security Intelligence Service
ten-foot pole, they will simply assign the job to the Defence of External Affairs security service and do indirectly what they cannot do directly. The motion by my friend from Vancouver South says "no way". All of these agencies have to go through the review committee so it will have a broad overview of what is going on and provide for some real accountability.
Make no bones about it, Mr. Speaker, this is a critical Bill. I regret that the NDP have sort of dissipated its importance by attacking everything equally. By applying some judgment to it, we should have forgotten about all the small clauses and honed in on the five or six critical areas. I think we could have more effectively convinced the Canadian people to go with us and put enough pressure on back-benchers on the other side that they could have stood against the Cabinet.

Mr. Speaker, my good friend, the Parliamentary Secretary, was there in committee. He contributed mightily to the committee's work by moving a motion that would have cut off any debate whatsoever on any amendments. He contributed a great deal and he talked to me about relevance. Let me say something about relevance. It was not a Member on this side who raised the issue of whether Mr. Turner agreed with closure. It was the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre who
raised it. All I was doing was giving my friends on the Government side the courtesy of responding to them.
There is another thing being done by this reform-minded Mr. Turner. Motion No. 96 is in the name of the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Kaplan). In the committee the only amendment of substance that was passed was one which said that the review committee should see the Cabinet documents that relate directly to the security service. That is what we managed to get done in committee. Now, with Mr. Turner's blessing, the Solicitor General comes in here a couple of days after this great reform convention-they are going to open this place up and let the fresh air in-with an amendment which would wipe out the only substantive amendment passed in committee. Some reform! As I said yesterday, it is not a new deal, it is the old deal writ large. We are going to be asking the Canadian public the simple question: Would you buy a used government from Mr. Turner? That is what they will be getting. That is what the issue will be in the coming campaign.
It is absolutely incredible. This Government tells us to get on with second reading, to get the Bill into committee, listen to the witnesses, make our motions for amendments, and the Government will give them due consideration. If there are sensible suggestions from sensible people they will listen and accept them if appropriate. We get an amendment in which finally gives the review committee what they absolutely have to have if they are going to be a review committee, and that is the right to see the orders from Cabinet. Sure, it was by accident because a Liberal Member was asleep in his chair, but we got it through nonetheless. But then what happened? The first thing Mr. Turner tells the Solicitor General to do this week is to get an amendment in to make sure there is no way in the world the review committee could ever look at what the Cabinet orders the agency to do.
This reminds me of the marvellous theory of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). In 1977 we asked what they had been doing after these revelations of wrongdoing. He said we do not need to worry about secret acts done in the night by the police, the courts will protect us. That is what that great law professor, the Right Hon. the Prime Minister, said. What a laughable notion that was and is. If there are secret things done by the police in the dark of night, the court will never hear about them so they cannot protect us. But that notion is alive and well in this Chamber. The Solicitor General is imbued with it, as is the pack of mummified creatures which represent their constituencies on the Government side. No matter how ancient they may be or what wisdom they may have accumulated, they are all wrapped in mummy clothing and all you will ever get out of them is dust from their old, staring faces. These are the people who are going to go along with this quaint notion of the Prime Minister. They will make absolutely sure of it because the new Leader has made sure that the only substantive amendment the Solicitor General has at report stage is to wipe out what we managed to do in committee. How can a review committee give the public any confidence that it will know what is going on if it cannot see those documents? The fact of


the matter is it cannot; the Government knows it but it just does not care.
