Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on Motions Nos. 93 through 97 which are presently before the House. We are now at the point in the deliberations of the House at which the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Kaplan) is attempting to reverse the one decision of substance by the committee to strengthen the provisions of this Bill. I emphasize that and hope that Members of the House are aware of exactly what is going on here. On a casting vote of the chairman of the Justice Committee the committee decided that the Security Intelligence Review Committee should have full access, at least to all of the documents which are in the possession of the security service itself. That was the decision of the Justice Committee.
I note that that decision was taken despite the fact that the former Solicitor General, the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), was yanked off the committee. Although he attended meeting after meeting of the committee and heard the witnesses that appeared before the committee, when it came to the tough decisions on voting, despite being the Solicitor General of this country for four years, the Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East was replaced by members of the Liberal Party who had never attended meetings of the Justice Committee.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Are you sure he did not ask to be taken off?
What a shameful manipulation of the committee-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Did he tell you he was yanked off?

-by members of the Government. Despite his expressed desire to vote on amendments, the Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East was pulled off the replaced by the trained seals on the other side.
On this motion the Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East said:
Mr. Chairman, the purpose of the review comittee was to give credibility to the Bill, to assure the public that there would be a balance between the needs for security and the needs for protection of civil rights and so on. There are not too many occasions when Cabinet documents will be the subject matter of review by the security service, or in their hands.
He went on to say:
But refusing to allow the review committee to examine them I think raises again more suspicions in the minds of the public. I have made this argument many, many times. I just cannot understand why we insist on preventing them-
That is a man who was the Solicitor General for four years. He is indicating that he has no idea why the Government is refusing access to these documents by the review committee. The chairman of the committee himself cast the deciding vote. The Liberal Member who chairs the committee said:
The chairman has reflected for a long time on this subject and has heard all arguments. The chairman has never been convinced by the Minister that there was reason for those documents in possession of the service not to be shown to


Security Intelligence Service
the oversight committee. For those reasons the chairman votes in favour of the amendment.
The amendment actually carried in committee. It was the one amendment of substance to be put before the committee and adopted. Now before the House the Solicitor General tells his trained seals that they do not want to accept the decision of the Justice Committee and tells them to reverse it. What insufferable arrogance on the part of the Solicitor General!
Professor Peter Russell was one of the many witnesses who appeared before the committee. The witnesses were virtually unanimous on the question of access to Cabinet documents by members of the review committee. Professor Russell said:
It is preposterous that some of the Queen's Privy Councillors cannot trust other of the Queen's Privy Councillors.
The Government that seeks our trust in establishing a civilian security agency under its direction must trust the watchdogs it will appoint on our behalf.
Those are the remarks of Professor Peter Russell. He talks of the sheer arrogance of the Government in this provision.
For once the committee was actually prepared to listen to the witnesses. Then the Government turns around and says to hell with the Justice Committee. Even though the Government puts its trained seals in, the committee will still be prepared to accept the amendment. But the Government is going to reverse what the Justice Committee did in the one area of substance. What a mockery of the independence of committees in the House!
The Senate committee was chaired by Michael Pitfield. He surely is not one lightly to disregard conventions of Cabinet secrecy and so on. Even the Senate committee strongly recommended this amendment. It unanimously recommended that the Security Intelligence Review Committee should have access to all documents, including Cabinet documents, in the possession of the security service. The Pitfield committee said:
As with the Inspector General, the SIRC should have access to all cabinet documents in the possession of the CSIS. Finally, the committee believes that the staffing of the SIRC is a very important matter and should be done with care to ensure that it is a small but effective body.
We can hear from the Minister's flunky, his Parliamentary Secretary, if he dares to stand up and defend this provision, if he is capable of defending this provision, which some of us doubt. We can hear from the Minister's flunky in due course.
However, the Pitfield committee makes it very clear that at least the review committee which is made up of Privy Councillors should be trusted by other Privy Councillors with documents in the possession of the security service. We reject the suggestion of the Minister that the decision of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs should be overturned and that secrecy should be the order of the day with respect to this review committee, particularly when the Government refuses to accept the recommendations of the McDonald Commission and the many witnesses who appeared before the committee. Parliament itself should play a role, not just to a group of handpicked former Privy Councillors. The Congress of the United States has trusted members of Congress to play a role in oversight.
The Government denies elected representatives the right to full and effective oversight and says that it is establishing a committee. But even though that committee will be made up of Privy Councillors, it will not be trusted with documents that are in the hands of the security service. What insufferable arrogance on the part of the Government. What denial of any meaningful oversight.
The motions before the House would also ensure that the relationships between the security service and any other bodies and agencies engaged in security or intelligence functions in Canada would also come under the umbrella of the review committee. Otherwise it will be all too easy for a government to evade its responsibility and evade the scrutiny of the oversight committee by in fact transferring responsibility from the Security Intelligence Service to some other shadowy intelligence agency that does not fall under the umbrella framework of this legislation.
Therefore, I urge Members of the House for once to display a little bit of independence. We know we cannot rely on the flunky, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister, to do so, but certainly I know that when the time comes to vote on this important motion perhaps there will be one or two Members on the other side of the House who will display some sense of integrity and dedication to the principles of effective oversight and will vote against the Solicitor General's motion.

Mr. Speaker, in joining this debate on the motions that are now before the House, I want to make some particular remarks about Motion No. 96 which deals with the amendments permitting greater access by the Security Intelligence Review Committee to information held by the Cabinet. One must consider this amendment in the context of the whole creation of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service and all that has gone on before in terms of freedom of information. Those are the general thoughts that I want to put on the record in the House.
First, the Government brought before the House of Commons a freedom of information Bill called the Access to Information Act. The purpose of the legislative measure was to throw light on information held by the Government and to make it of a public nature, to the extent that it was in the public interest to do so. The principle that was adopted by the Parliament of Canada in enacting the access to information legislation was to allow sunshine to come into the government arena so that those who needed information from the Government for whatever purpose could obtain that information. That was a principle that was endorsed almost unanimously by the House of Commons. It is in that context that we must approach any attempt to keep information held by the Government secret.
We must start with the premise that all information should be public and that there must be very serious reasons for keeping information away from the public in general terms. The point I want to make is that the Government and the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan), in dealing with this matter of access to information by the Security Intelligence Review Committee has not only disregarded the general principle of


access to information but has disregarded the real need for access to information in this particular circumstance.
The public concern about a Security Intelligence Service for Canada is that the powers given to a service and the officers employed in such a service can be abused. The only safeguard against that kind of abuse is a review by some authority independent of the Security Intelligence Service. If that authority, which is the Security Intelligence Service Review Committee in this case, has its powers hampered by unnecessary legislative constraints and restrictions it will simply not be able to carry out its task.
What is more important is the signal that this kind of legislation amendment gives to those who are deeply and properly concerned about security intelligence legislation. The signal that is sent out by the kind of legislation amendment that is now being demanded by the Solicitor General is that the Government does not intend to have free access to information in this area of the review of the Security Intelligence Service. It wants to allow matters to be covered up, hidden away or obscured. That is entirely inconsistent with the purpose of a review committee. If the review committee has anything hidden from its purview and has any restrictions placed upon its access to information that relates to the operation of the security intelligence service, then that committee will not have the kind of power and authority that is essential to carry out its mandated function.
In simple terms, if the ability of a review committee to search out facts is going to be restricted, then there might as well not be a review committee. Those who want to hide the facts will simply hide them under that particular carpet. They will find ways to characterize and classify information as falling within the exception to the rule of access rather than to falling in the general right to access to information.
Those are the kinds of games that government officers throughout the bureaucracy of the Government of Canada has been playing in the last 16 years. The minute that a method is provided to hide information from those who would otherwise have a right of access to that information, they will use that exemption to hide that information in question. If Members doubt the ability of bureaucrats to utilize that kind of provision, I can say, after a number of years of experience in dealing with these matters, that that is exactly what they do. How do you think the Department of Finance hides away information concerning the finances of Canada? How do you think Revenue Canada hides away processes and procedures that it follows, as we have seen demonstrated time and time again? It is all under the claim of exemption and under a claim that there is no need for the public to have knowledge of that particular action. It is always under some statutory exemption or colour of right. That is what the Solicitor General is giving to the Canadian Security Intelligence Service. He is giving the service the colour of right to hide away information from the review committee. In that way the Solicitor General is destroying the whole purpose and raison d'etre of that review committee.
Security Intelligence Service
I believe we must stand and point out these matters. In my view, the public is not interested in this Bill in the way it has been presented to the House of Commons. There is no urgency. The only urgency is the empty space a few streets away from the House of Commons that the Solicitor General had rented for the Security Intelligence Service. There is no need to have a Security Intelligence Service this month as opposed to the next month or the month after. It is a false sense of urgency attached to the presentation of this Bill in the House of Commons. That false sense of urgency has been used as an excuse for such steps as closure that has been forced upon the House of Commons in relation to its deliberations on Bill C-9.
It is that idea of urgency that excuses the Government's action in invoking closure in this situation. But that will not wash with the people of Canada. There is nobody out there waiting for the establishment of the Canadian Intelligence Security Service, waiting for it to catch spies and to stop the espionage that may or may not be taking place in Canada. I do not know of one person who has approached me and said: "Get the Canadian Security Intelligence Service into operation before the Government and the country collapses". That false sense of urgency is in the big lie category that we have to get this service in operation quickly to save the country. That is nonsense. That is the kind of unnecessary speed and haste that can cause grave difficulties in the future. That is the kind of speed and haste that causes Parliament and parliamentarians to overlook the real problems that are involved in the Canadian Security Intelligence Service and the legislation relating to it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Fifteen years is speed and haste?
The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) has come to my aid again. He says it has been sixteen years in the making.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Fifteen years.

Why has it been fifteen years in the making? Because the people of Canada have not reached any consensus on the matter. I defy the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) who comes from the heart of Toronto and I defy the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre to tell me what the views are in British Columbia, Nova Scotia or in other parts of Canada on a Canadian security intelligence service.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: You just told us you don't know.

If the Minister thinks the people of British Columbia are waiting for this service to come into operation, he is wrong. If the Solicitor General thinks the people of Canada want civil liberties set aside and the RCMP downgraded and denigrated in order to rush through the Canadian Security Intelligence Service, he is wrong. But it just indicates once more that there is no communication between this Government of Canada and the people. It proves once again that that line of communication has been destroyed. The Govern-


Security Intelligence Service
ment does not know what the Canadian people are thinking. This is just one more dramatic illustration that the Government is out of touch with the needs of the people.
We are standing here in the House of Commons debating security intelligence legislation when we should be talking about job creation, about improving the Canadian economy and about getting people back to work.
You should have passed it a long time ago.

We cannot stop the debate just because we are forced into that situation by the Government of Canada and by members of the Liberal Party. We cannot stop and we cannot give up on civil liberties. We cannot give up on a national institution like the RCMP merely because the Government of Canada has created a situation in Parliament that offends our sense of Parliamentary democracy.

Mr. Speaker, in addressing the motions currently under consideration, I have to say that I have not heard as much gobbledegook in a long, long time as I have heard parroted from the Government benches in the last few minutes.
In one of the motions we are trying to restore by amendment one of the actions taken by the Justice Committee. All we get is shouting from the other side about how they have been waiting to do this for 16 years, and how this great demand is out there in the Canadian public to have a new security service, outside of the RCMP, with unheard of powers, unheard of in this country, unheard of in almost every other western country. In fact, it is totally unheard of.
While we are concerned about the details, we are also concerned as to the state of mind and the thrust that lies behind the Bill, particularly the willingness on the part of the Government to trample over the wishes of even its own Members on the Justice Committee, not to mention the feelings of other Members in all the Parties of the House. Within all Parties there are a number of serious reservations when we are dealing with legislation such as this and with motions such as these that deal with the review system.
Let us look at who makes up the review committee. Clause 34, which has been dealt with previously, reads:
34.(1) There is hereby established a committee, to be known as the Security Intelligence Review Committee, consisting of a Chairman and not less than two and not more than four other members, all of whom shall be appointed by the Governor in Council from among members of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada who are not members of the Senate or the House of Commons, after consultation by the Prime Minister of Canada with the Leader of the Opposition in the House of Commons and the leader in the House of Commons of each party having at least twelve members in that House.
If the Government is not prepared to have a body such as that, Mr. Speaker-and I would ask Hon. Members to take a look at all of the documents to which the committee felt it should have access-review all documents, then who the devil is to be trusted in the country in the Government's view? Is the Government saying that the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) judgment is not to be trusted, even when he had consulted with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) and in consultation with the Leader of our Party? Is the Government saying that the Government's own Prime Minister who appoints these people is not to be trusted, or that other review committee members who are members of the Privy Council are not to be trusted with all of the information to which the Justice Committee thought it should have access? What absolute hogwash that is. These guys have gone right off the deep end. There is no public demand for this legislation.
On the other hand we have the Attorney General of every province in Canada opposed to the legislation, we have civil liberties groups, the Canadian Medical Association, everyone left, right and centre right across the whole spectrum of Canadian political opinion who think this is bad law. The Liberals apparently do not trust their own Prime Minister, even in consultation with Leaders of the other Parties on this.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.

You don't trust him. That is obvious and that is why the Government has brought in this amendment to overrule the feeling of the Justice Committee. If the Liberals do not trust whomever their own Prime Minister appoints, whom can they trust? Nobody. I do not blame them for not trusting him. I do not have a lot of faith in them over there either.
We have to ask ourselves again, if the Liberals are that imbalanced and if they are that topsy-turvy in their system of priorities. What is their state of mind and why?
My mind goes back a couple of months ago. I along with one Member of the Conservative Party, Gerard Docquier, President of the Canadian district of the United Steel Workers, and John Fryer, President of the National Union of Provincial Government Employees, attended a meeting about two blocks away from Parliament Hill of a group called the Niagara Institute. With the exception of the four of us whom I have just mentioned, the rest were chief executive officers of some of the major corporations and banks in Canada. A question was posed during the discussion. Their answer was virtually unanimous to the query: "When will a condition approaching economic normalcy be restored in Canada?" The assessment by thes chief executive officers was that it will come about in 35 to 50 years.
Is that the kind of agenda to which the Government is going to succumb in this country? Does it agree that that is the state of affairs we will have-unemployment ranging from 10 per cent up to somewhere in the 20 per cent range for the next 35 or 50 years? Those people in the board rooms are mostly the same people who dominate the major councils of the Liberal Party. Have they decided to surrender to that agenda? It is not what anybody wants, but are they going to surrender to it? That is the prediction, unless the Government takes a totally different approach from that which it had heretofore since Confederation. If that is to happen, and if that Government continues to be totally derelict in its responsibilities to do something about the basic economic and social conditions which that situation will create, then it may need some of these kinds of powers to stop civil unrest. Is that the Government's


agenda? Has the Government admitted its failure and the only way the Liberals and their pals can continue to govern is by setting up the agencies of a police state? That is how this service can be used. Why else would the Liberals not accept even minimal amendments such as those proposed by the Justice Committee? Why else would they not propose some of the very minimal amendments that both my colleagues in the Conservative Party and my colleagues in the New Democratic Party are proposing? Why else? Nobody suggests that you over there are a bunch of bad guys. But are you so blind to the economic realities facing this country that you have come to accept the idea that we will see the same kind of growth of terrorism here as we have seen in Europe? God forbid. We have been immune from that so far. Are the Liberals surrendering to that possibility? Are they surrendering to the possibility that people will be continuously unemployed across the country over a 35-year to 50-year period and will be upset? No? Why then do they need the powers outlined in the Bill?
I see no reason. No one demanded it. Nobody aside from a self-appointed commission has ever recommended any of the proposals, and what that commission recommended did not go as far as the proposals in this Bill. The Government does not listen to the appointed members of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. It does not listen to anyone.
The Government has its own agenda. Whether it is a hidden agenda or a public agenda, it stinks and it is rotten. It ought to call a halt to this business and get on with the real priorities- the economic and social issues on which the people of this country are demanding action. The Government should give up. It is a failure.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak about one aspect of the group of motions before us, the abuse of the concept of Crown privilege. Canada is a monarchy. Most Canadians, whether or not they are enthusiastic monarchists, accept and rely upon the concept of our traditional form of government for both a sense of stability and a sense of fair play. Of course there have often been failures in that regard, but that is the system which is available and it is the one Canadians continue to support and choose. I do not think any one of us is aware of any likelihood of getting rid of it.
The Government is proposing a very serious action which will discredit the concept of Crown privileges. It is not the first time the Government has taken actions to discredit the Crown. However, on this occasion it is more serious. It goes much deeper than the other actions. It is much worse than the abuse of privilege when VIA Rail rode roughshod over Parliament. It is much worse than the abuse of privilege when the Government said that because a Crown corporation took part in a uranium price-fixing cartel, the cartel could not be investigated by the courts. The then Minister of Justice sneered at Parliament and said that we could not investigate the Crown.
When a matter concerns the fundamental liberties of Canadians, not one enterprise or another or a particular part
Security Intelligence Service
of the economy, a matter which may be crucial to the actions of the security service, it cannot be examined by the watchdog appointed by that service nor by the watchdog committee appointed for that purpose, even though they are appointed by the Chief Minister of the Crown. In doing this the Government discredits the Crown in other respects. For example, it discredits the report of Senator Pitfield which soberly indicated that the committee ought to have access to Crown documents among others.
The Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) assured us that there were no Crown documents in the possession of the security service. However, he did not tell us why he was afraid of the recommendation of the committee and he wanted to reverse it. Other commissions appointed under the Crown, such as the McDonald Commission, have also indicated that there should be oversight, including oversight of Crown documents.
Public leaders have spoken on this matter, such as the United Church, the Canadian Council of Churches, labour groups and civil liberties groups. They all feel, with due respect for the basic privilege of the Crown, that it should not be used in this way. The chairman of the committee appointed by the Chief Minister of the Crown and the committee as a whole thought that privilege should not be used in this way. However, the Solicitor General, again in the name of the Crown, overruled them.
For the average man or woman on the street, it is very demoralizing to see the concept of the Crown and the name of the Crown or Crown privilege being turned into nothing more than the privilege of a tiny group of men and women who happen at one time to have responsibility under the Crown. For this to be turned into a weapon that they can use against other agencies of the Crown and all other people who have sworn to uphold the laws of the land, such as Hon. Members of the House and of the other place, makes a mockery of the Crown. That one little group is now grasping the power to deny the obligations of the Crown as they are expressed through Members of Parliament in this place and in the Senate and other public groups established in the name of the Crown. Only one secret group will be allowed that Crown privilege, will be allowed to look at Crown documents, which may affect the liberties of Canadians in a fundamental way that we have never before experienced in the history of Canada.
We are told that some privy Councillors will and must distrust other Privy Councillors. That makes a mockery of the Crown. Apparently this tiny group of men has the power to do this and get away with it. They have been able to wrench the rules of Parliament and of committee. They have been able to drive through their points, notwithstanding the fact that the Opposition had been operating according to the rules. They simply changed the rules when it suited them. They can get away with it, but they do damage to the public morale and the public trust in the Crown which will take years and years to mend.
When the public begins to understand the contemptuous way in which the Solicitor General and his colleagues have


Security Intelligence Service
abused the concept of the Crown, it will not be an easy matter for the Government or any other succeeding government to win the support and trust of the people of Canada. Perhaps the damage is not irreparable, but it will not be repaired for many years to come. It is regrettable that the Solicitor General and his colleagues have acted so irresponsibly as to insist upon reintroducing this abusive use of the Crown privilege.

Mr. Speaker, I will make my comments very brief. The Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) has called us contemptible. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to add my objections to those of the many other Members who spoke this afternoon. The Government is attempting to undo the work of the committee. Certainly there are several clauses in this particular Bill which have received a great deal of attention, and rightly so. Civil libertarians, most people who are involved, have experience and will be affected by this Bill, have spoken against those clauses, certainly Clause 39. It has been said many times that the Government watchdog, even though it may be a sleeping watchdog, should have access to Cabinet documents, not all, just those that are relevant. The reason why civil libertarians and others zeroed in on this clause is that they recognize that if the watchdog committee does not have access to these documents, a great deal of harm might flow from that.
In most countries of the world where people's rights have been restricted, downtrodden, stepped upon and trampled on, this invariably started through political activity. Unfortunately, governments such as this which have been in power for a long time gain in arrogance, they have a feeling that they govern by the grace of God, by Divine right. If there is objection or opposition to those governments, they take away the rights of certain citizens on the grounds that it is good for the public as a whole. They want to maintain the public good, as it were.
In many countries in Europe, Asia and Africa this type of slow and steady erosion of the rights of individuals has occurred. Unfortunately, it is usually done in the name of the law. That is the kind of loophole that Clause 39 creates for this Government. With all due respect, this Government has had a lot of experience in trodding on the rights of others. Historically, this Government has shown that it panics very quickly. We need only look back to the imposition of the War Measures Act, that phoney revolution that was about to happen in Quebec, to see how quickly that can happen. This type of clause leaves it wide open for the Government to instruct this secret service, these super snoopers, to go beyond the bounds of propriety and investigate things they should not investigate. Even then the watchdog committee will not have access to those instructions. It will never know about them. Parliament may never know. That is something this Government should not allow. The people of Canada are very much opposed to this potential abuse of the civil liberties of Canadians.
It would not have been as bad if the Government had agreed to a tighter definition of Clause 2 to ensure that the secret service had to work within the legal bounds of strict control and had not allowed it to use subversive techniques on those who had not committed a crime. Clause 2(d) in particular is causing much trouble. Then it might not have been as bad that the Government is insisting that the watchdog committee cannot investigate Cabinet documents. However, the Government has not done that. It has not done a lot of things it should have done and which the people of Canada have pleaded with it to do. In its own arrogance, it really believes it is right.
I find it difficult to understand how the Government arrived at that conclusion. In the last four years this Government has done almost nothing right. This Parliament will end in a short while and we will be left with this document. It is a document which is mightily flawed. If Clause 39 is amended as the Government is attempting to amend it, the document will be that much worse.
It bears repeating that the reason the Government has to amend this clause is that the Chairman of the committee voted against the Government. Had the normal complement of Government Members been there, the Chairman would not have had to vote. This Government is so disorganized, uninterested and lacking in will to proceed that it could not raise the number of voting members to ensure that it got its wish, so the Chairman had to vote. He is a very fair Chairman. On many occasions he said he did not like this clause and, therefore, he voted against the Government. That is the committee system at work. That is the whole purpose of it. One would expect the Government to accept something of that nature, but it does not. It abuses the whole process. Why should we waste our time in committee, sitting there hour after hour after hour? Why should the people of Canada spend hours appearing before that committee when the Government uses its powers to steamroll over what the committee proposes? On one hand the Government says it will accept what the committee does, but only in those situations where it gets its wish. Where it does not get its way, it does not accept what the committee does.


The Government tries to have it both ways. I suspect that it will succeed in having its own way for the next six or seven days.
It was said earlier that the people of Canada will remember this. They are very concerned about their rights. They are concerned that this legislation has the potential to damage the freedoms that have been developed in Canada over the past 170 years. It is incumbent on the Government before this day is out to withdraw its objection to the watchdog committee having the opportunity to review Cabinet documents. It may well be a sleeping dog committee because it will not be a committee of elected members, as proposed by most people. It could have allowed a parliamentary committee. Parliamentarians respond to the desires, wishes and fears of their constituents. Perhaps then Clause 39 would not be so bad, but the Government has not done that. It pushed aside every opportunity to make this a good Bill, one which would secure the rights of Canadians and at the same time allow the security service to do that which is necessary. The Government has not done that, and it is not likely it will.
There is one last opportunity for the Minister to correct this Bill. Perhaps he will do that. The Government could then leave this Parliament in the next few days having done at least something worth-while, namely, provided security legislation that is not a threat to every person in this country.

Mr. Speaker, a government should want its legislation to be effective. Looking at the amendment of the Hon. Member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser), I do not understand how anyone who wants proper legislation and the proper operation of a civilian or RCMP corps can vote against this motion. The motion was presented by the Hon. Member for Vancouver South. He is an experienced parliamentarian, having been in the House of Commons for many years. As a Cabinet Minister, I had the greatest respect for him. He found time to talk to the people and tried to reflect their thinking. That is democracy. I have the highest regard for him. He is trained in the law, practised law in Vancouver, was solicitor for municipalities as well as individuals. With his background, when he presents a motion, it should carry some weight. That is why I find it difficult to understand the reaction to Motion No. 94 to amend Clause 38.
I shall read the motion that we are now asking this House to adopt. If any Hon. Member in the House can give me one reason why this motion should not be passed, I will accept it. However, I cannot conceive of one reason why it should not be passed. This motion deals with the duties of the review committee. Clause 38 describes the functions of the review committee and this motion would add the following to those functions:
-to review, generally, the effectiveness and the propriety of Canada's security and intelligence functions and arrangements, including such functions as are carried on by any agency, department or institution of the Government of Canada;-
Security Intelligence Service
We are simply asking the review committee to look at the effectiveness and propriety of the functions and arrangements of the Security Intelligence Service. If anyone thinks that we do not need to include in the wording of it both "effectiveness" and "propriety", I would counter by suggesting a reason why we do need them both. Something can be effective and not proper. Something can be proper and not effective. I am concerned that under this clause, this committee should have the responsibility to review the functions of this intelligence service to find out if it is effective and is doing the job.
When I was the principal of a school, at the end of every month, and sometimes more frequently, I took an inventory of what the teachers were doing, what was effective and what was not effective. In a classroom, we would discuss why the particular method being used was or was not effective. For example, if a teacher was teaching arithmetic to a youngster in either grade one, two or three and the youngster was simply not learning how to add or multiply, I would say to his teacher: "His mother tells me that he cannot multiply and that he does not understand multiplication. What method are you using to teach him how to multiply?" The teacher would be very co-operative and would review her methods. She would say to me: "I will find out what I am doing wrong or if I am not spending enough time with the child." The following week she would say: "I know what was wrong. I was going over the subject too fast and Johnnie is a slow learner. I have to go through it three or four or five times with Johnnie before he begins to understand what I am trying to do." An owner of a business must check to see whether or not his methods are effective. Are people coming into his shop and buying his products? If they are, his advertising is effective. If they are not, it is not effective and he must make a change. I would think a Government would also check to find out whether or not it is being effective.
The motion of the Hon. Member for Vancouver South is only asking that the effectiveness of the methods of the security service be reviewed. If the methods are not effective, we should not waste the people's money. Who in this House could vote against that? Surely we want to get full value for every dollar spent. Not even the most extravagant Liberal member would not want government agencies to be effective.
The other key word in the motion is "propriety". We want the committee to review the propriety of the functions of the security service as well. We want it to review its functions to see whether or not it is acting in accordance with good behaviour and good morals. Take the War Measures Act of 1970, for example. It was certainly effective, but was it proper? Was it right to shove scores of people into jail without a trial when they had committed no offence? Some of the people were never even charged at all but were shoved into jail like cattle. The War Measures Act might have been effective but it would not pass a review of propriety because none of us believe in shoving people into jail without even giving them a chance to defend themselves. That is something that can take place. This civilian intelligence service is a body which is being


Security Intelligence Service
given pretty wide powers. We should make sure that its actions are effective, proper and morally right.
The new Leader of the Liberal Party has indicated that he wants to make more use of committees and that he wants to have free votes. I will believe that when I see it. A committee has made a recommendation, but the Government is now going to change that recommendation because it does not agree with it even though its own members supported it. The committee's representations reflected the combined thinking of members of the committee. The new Leader says he will make more use of back-benchers, but will he then have the Cabinet overrule them and tell other Members that that cannot go on, that he will change it and wipe it out? I do not think that that is an effective way to administer a country. If we are going to have such things as committees, then surely the combined consensus of that committee should be accepted, particularly when scores of recommendations were made by people who appeared before it.
What else does this motion attempt to do? I shall read it again:
-to review, generally, the effectiveness and the propriety of Canada's security and intelligence functions and arrangements, including such functions as are carried on by any agency, department or institution of the Government of Canada;-
Does anyone here want to see an agency or Department behave badly, ineffectively and with bad morals? If not, there is no reason in the world why Hon. Members should not vote for this motion. We want effective administration and we want it to have good behaviour and good morals. I would say to Hon. Government Members that if they vote this motion down, they are indicating that they do not want full value for money spent, that they want to do things immorally and that they want to do things that are not proper, and that cannot be called good behaviour. I think every Member of the House should support this motion which has been carefully and excellently phrased by the Hon. Member for Vancouver South.

Mr. Speaker, I take part in this debate after having read Barbara Tuchman's book dealing with power. I would like to engage the attention of the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) and draw to his attention the whole matter of review and accountability.
My colleagues, the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) and the Hon. Member for Kootenay West (Mr. Kristiansen), have expressed their points of view, with which I fully agree. I would like to ask the Solicitor General if he would think about and learn from history so that we do not repeat history.
None of us in this place believe that we act as rubber stamps. None of us wish to act that way or will act that way. I give that much credit to all Members of this House. I would like to suggest to the Solicitor General that in the case of accountability and review of the service, he consider that someone somewhere must tell all Canadians what is going on in the way of security, surveillance, intelligence and the like. If the hon. gentleman has not read Barbara Tuchman's writings, he should read them. I have reread them. The German Reichstag, the Italian Parliament, the Parliament in Spain, and even the Supreme Soviet of the Soviet Union had their parliaments blindly and supinely agree to all the things which went on in those nations before the First World War-in the 1920s and in the 1930s.
In the situation in which we find ourselves in Canada, why would the Solicitor General refuse to accept amendments which attempt to guard against that kind of repetition of history? I can understand small countries which are in the midst of terrible war situations being extra careful and extra militant. But why would we want to bring upon ourselves, in this nation, in the context of the security of Canada, an opportunity for those who would destroy us on the left or on the right as had happened in previous decades?
The Hon. Member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) made the mistake of mentioning the War Measures Act. I believe the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) did the same. They should at least have had the courtesy to blush. In 1970 only one Conservative stood up with the NDP caucus to vote against the War Measures Act. The rest of the Conservative Party voted for its implementation. That was nothing more than a symptom of the disease with which the Solicitor General is afflicted. It is a symptom of the kind of paranoia which wants to put the entire Canadian population into a situation as though we were a major power in the world, which we are not. We account for a lot of things on this planet, but in no way are we in the kind of major leagues in which the Solicitor General feels that this country should be trying to play. He wants to play in a major league with champagne measures for a beer operation.
If we are to learn anything at all from history, it should be the fear and the worry that cause us in our caucus, having learned those lessons not only in other countries but in our own nation, that what may be acceptable now, and what I think is acceptable now, was unacceptable in the 1920s and 1930s in Canada. It was the people who said that we must do something about getting rid of that foreign element who turned the RCMP on to trade union leaders, leaders of ethnic groups and political leaders including plainchothesmen who followed J. S. Woodsworth around. Surely the Solicitor General must know and understand this as well or better than I do.
I think it was Pastor Niemoeller who indicated that one did not tend to protest when laws and regulations such as this one were passed. He said:
In Germany they came first for the Communists, and I didn't speak up because I wasn't a Communist. Then they came for the Jews, and I didn't speak up because I wasn't a Jew. Then they came for the trade unionists, and I didn't speak up because I wasn't a trade unionist. Then they came for the Catholics, and I didn't speak up because I was a Protestant. Then they came for me, and by that time no one was left to speak up.
It would seem to me that any open and democratic society must deal with threats to its security, sovereignty and right to keep secret whatever is worth keeping secret. Democratic societies must face the risk and the threat, even after the fact. There cannot be anybody in a democratic and open society



with the authority to investigate the lives of anyone and everyone for whatever reason without having to account to this place and to the people of the country, even if it means the breaking of the oath of secrecy by a Privy Councillor. I would like to see a review committee which-if it decided against a procedure or action under this kind of legislation-would resign en masse and state why. I would like to see that happen with individual Members. This is nothing more than some kind of a desire by the Solicitor General to become a 007. He wants to join in with the CIA and the 15 intelligence agencies in the United States. The United States cannot even keep track of all of them.
Mr. Speaker, me thinks he doth worry too much. Any secrets which we have, our potential enemies already have. I would cite to the Minister the case which took place when we were dealing with the Elections Expenses Act. I was attempting to obtain the telephone numbers of National Defence personnel and Armed Forces personnel stationed at various bases around the world. I was told that it was top secret information. Then I obtained a copy of the Canadian Armed Forces magazine which published all of the telephone numbers-
Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but his time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to enter this debate. I think it is a crucial and historical debate for the country and for the House of Commons. The question which is before us is: How do we achieve security and peace in this country for the population? Do we do that through adding more police, and more investigators, or do we do that by giving a broader mandate to security agencies? Do we do that by giving a blanket mandate to a new civilian security agency, or, are there other ways of giving Canadians a sense of security?
The legislation before us poses some very serious questions. It gives very broad powers to a security agency and it has very weak oversight provisions. There are very weak checks and balances for those powers. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the giving of very broad investigatory powers to an agency without appropriate checks and balances is bound to increase the strife and insecurity in this nation rather than decrease it. We are living in a time when tensions in our society are increasing by virtue of the inequality in income and benefits which exists in our country. All of us in this House are aware, Mr. Speaker, that the top 20 per cent of the population, for example, receives something like 40 per cent of the total income, while the bottom 20 per cent receives something like 4 per cent of the total income. With inequities like this, there are bound to be social tensions in this country calling attention to the injustices which exist, and there are bound to be political movements calling for change.
The relevance of that sociological comment to the present legislation, Mr. Speaker, is that we must be careful to make a
Security Intelligence Service
distinction between dissent and subversion. If we are to make that distinction, Mr. Speaker, it must not only be made very clearly in legislation which sets out a limited mandate for a security agency but we must also observe this distinction in the administration of that agency. The only way we can observe the distinction between subversion and legitimate political dissent is by having a group which can oversee the actions of this agency.
The legislation before us today falls far short of the requirements with regard to oversight. What we need in this country is parliamentary oversight of any security activity which is going on in the country. This legislation does not provide for that. It provides another form of oversight which is extremely limited. The clause before us indicates how limited that oversight is. This committee, which would be appointed by the Government rather than by Parliament, could not even review all of the documents which would be in the hands of the security agency itself. Therefore, the security agency, in terms of access to information, would be above the review committee. That is a fundamental flaw and it will tend to lead to further distrust in the public's mind with regard to the activities of the security agency.
This legislation poses serious questions for us today because, Mr. Speaker, there are many people in this country who are seeking, through legitimate political means, to bring about a greater measure of social justice, whether they are involved in the native movement, the peace movement or are recent immigrants to this country. For example, there are immigrants to this country from Latin America who are interested in global justice. It is important that these people be given the assurance that an agency such as this will not abuse its authority and in any blanket way investigate anyone who goes on a peace march, or anyone who speaks out on behalf of the native community for social justice in this country, or any members of the Latin American community or the Chilean community who choose to speak out against the injustices of a regime such as the Pinochet regime which exists in Chile today.
I am blowing the whistle on the actions of this Government today, Mr. Speaker, because what it is doing is setting in place a police agency with very broad powers without adequate checks and balances. It is important, Mr. Speaker, that the checks and balances be there if we are going to give these kinds of powers to any agency in this country. We know from Canadian history, and American history as well, that it is possible to abuse power. We must learn from that history and we must guard against the abuse of power. I think specifically of the McCarthy era in the United States when people were labelled as communists and their careers ruined. Intimidation was used to prevent people from speaking out in legitimate political dissent. It is important that we learn from history that it is possible for Government and its agencies to abuse power. We must set in place the safeguards which will protect us from this potential abuse of power.
This legislation, Mr. Speaker, is fatally flawed and should be changed before the Government seeks passage of it in this


Security Intelligence Service
House. We are moving into an era of Canadian history which demands an act of citizenry, which demands that Canadians speak out against social injustice in this country. In these times we need a more active citizenry. We need people to speak out more forcefully on the maldistribution of income in this country, about the fact that the needs of the native people of this country are not adequately met, and about the fact that we continue to live under the threat of the nuclear arms race. This is not a time to give untrammelled powers to an agency. It is not a time to set up a situation which might lead to the intimidation of people in order to stop legitimate political dissent.
This is a time for sober second thought. That is not an original notion of mine, Mr. Speaker. In fact, the Senate has already taken that sober second thought and said, "Hold on, government of the day. Do not rush forward with this legislation. Amend it and amend it adequately before you present it to the House of Commons and to the public for approval". Therefore, I want to say quite simply, Mr. Speaker, that what we must do today is to sound the alarm. We must let every citizen in this country know that the Government has failed so far to put in place adequate safeguards against the abuse of power by this new security agency which it wishes to establish. There is no way that this legislation should be allowed to pass in this House without the Government changing the legislation and putting in place adequate safeguards. I call upon this Government and on any Hon. Members of the Liberal caucus who have the integrity to stand by their conscience, to-
There are not too many of them.

Well, hopefully, as the debate contines, there will be at least some Members in the back benches of the Liberal Party who will stand up and say to their own Minister, "Look, we take a long-term view of legislation and we do not think that any legislation which grants greater powers to a police agency should go into force without our putting in adequate safeguards".
So I would call upon this Government to put in place a parliamentary review committee to review the actions of this new security agency which is going to be established. I do not say these words lightly. There are too many people in this country who see the social problems which cry for attention and upon which they speak out. There is no way we should put in place an agency which might at some point abuse its power and serve to intimidate legitimate political dissent. I make the point, Mr. Speaker, that we must draw the line between subversive activities and legitimate political dissent. That line has not been drawn well enough, and as long as that is so, we draw the line and say, "no legislation".

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have sat here for several days now listening attentively to the debate, the interventions of the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) and the contributions largely from this side of the House. I do not believe there is very much I can say, or that needs to be said by myself, with respect to this legislation. The objections we have to it have been thoughtfully and
forcefully put in front of the House. I did not intend to enter the debate until my friend, the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), made an observation taken from a well known internationalist. I could not help thinking as he was speaking of an experience which I had, and I wish the Solicitor General could spend half a moment with me because I want to discuss Bupindhat Liddar for a moment or two. In the 20 years that I have been in this Chamber I have done one or two things I have not been proud of. A moment of rationalization could excuse the thoughtless way in which I as an individual-I will not speak for my colleagues because of course I cannot- approached the War Measures Act in the early 1970s. I made a mistake and I said so at the time, or shortly after the event. I believe I made another mistake in the summer of 1980. I was called to the residence of my then Leader, the Righ Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark). After a conversation with him, I had an obligation to call the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) further to the subject matter. I did so and, with his counsel and approval, I went further. The consequence of those meetings was to sever the relationship I had with a very bright and intelligent young man who had a good Canadian career ahead of him. He was a landed immigrant. His great fault was that he had an affinity for the PLO and some friends of his were close to it.
On the advice of my Leader, the Solicitor General, and the intelligence force that operated at that level, I severed that relationship. I invited that young man to leave Parliament Hill. That is history, but I recite it because I want to draw to the attention of Hon. Members the difficulty that we can sometimes find ourselves in when we do not have access to information we know we can trust. My conscience is troubled because I was the instrument that forced that young man to leave Canada. He had been in Canada for seven or eight years. He went back to what was then Rhodesia and is now Zimbabwe. He is currently living there trying to eke out a living. He wants to be a Canadian and I denied him that opportunity. I did so, as I mentioned, on the advice of others. I take the liberty of mentioning this, without going into detail because much of it is confidential, to say that on reflection the evidence I was given was not enough to warrant the action I took. Together with a distinguished former colleague in this Chamber, now a Member of the other place, we intend to try to correct that error as nearly as we can.
I do not know what the information was on this individual and I have no way of finding out. I have no way of demonstrating to my satisfaction that in fact the reasons that forced this young man to leave Canada were accurate; that it was not anything other than an attack on his empathy, if you will, for those Arabs in that part of the world who were having problems and difficulties. We must always be careful. It was too easy for me to simply say, "yes, if that is so, then I must act". That was the simple, easy way, but I regret having taken it. I regret that in legislation such as is before us now there is not some capacity for even that form of post factum examination. If documents or files could be looked at even five or ten


years after the fact, if the file were to be examined some day, then those who put the directives together and who carry out the activity would have to think twice. They would know that their actions would be reviewed, not necessarily in the context of the time of the act itself but at some point. I apologize, in a sense, for raising this matter, but, strangely enough, I feel a little better. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Pursuant to Section 11 of Standing Order 79, the recorded division on the proposed motion stands deferred.
The House will now consider Motions Nos. 99, 100, 101 and 102 which have been grouped for debate.

Motion No. 99
That Bill C-9 be amended by deleting Clause 41.
Motion No. 100
That Bill C-9 be amended in Clause 41 by striking out lines 22 to 25 at page 20 and substituting the following therefor:
"dissatisfied with the response given."
Motion No. 101
That Bill C-9 be amended by deleting Clause 42.
Motion No. 102
That Bill C-9 be amended in Clause 42
(a)	by striking out lines 32 to 34 at page 20 and substituting the following
therefor:
"42.(1) Where the denial of a security clearance required by the Government of Canada is a factor in a decision made"
(b)	by striking out lines 42 to 45 at page 20 and substituting the following
therefor:
Security Intelligence Service "(2) Where the denial of a security clearance required by the Government of Canada to be given in respect of an individual is a factor in a
decision made to deny the".
He said: Mr. Speaker, the clauses which are now before the House with regard to this security legislation and are the subject of the motions before the House at this time are Clauses 41 and 42. These clauses deal with the question of security checks and the role which is to be played by the proposed Security Intelligence Review Committee on the question of security checks.
I will commence my brief remarks on this series of motions by noting that in 1982, which is the last year for which we have figures, the RCMP security service ran some 76,500 security checks on public servants and employees in defence industries. This massive number of security checks has been described by the head of the Canadian Human Rights Commission, Mr. Gordon Fairweather, as a glorius waste of people's time. Not only is it a waste of people's time, it is obviously a considerable waste of taxpayers' money. Mr. Fair-weather noted that unnecessary security clearances, unnecessarily high levels of classification, and unnecessary snooping into the lives of individuals are not only wasteful of our resources, not only morally repugnant, but they are discriminatory. Of course that is absolutely right.
One of the purposes of the series of amendments which were put before the House on this occasion is to put some semblance of order into the security assessment process. First, it would significantly narrow the circumstances in which security assessments can be ordered. As I have indicated, there are far too many at the present time. Second, it would require that the criteria for security assessments be clearly set out in statutory form or, at the very least, in regulatory form. As it stands now, security assessments in the country are governed by a 1963 Cabinet directive which is completely out of date and out of keeping with present conditions. That is the first recommendation of substance. The criteria for security assessment should be spelled out and updated.
As well, the question of security assessment should be subject to review by the Security Intelligence Review Committee. In that regard, I would note that the amendments in question would strengthen that review process. As it stands now, Clause 42, for example, indicates that where, by reason only of the denial of the security clearance required by the Government of Canada, a decision is made to dismiss, demote or transfer, etc., the appeal mechanism set out in the Act is available. That clearly provides an out for the Government or Deputy Minister or whoever wants to fire, not hire, or not promote an individual. They have to say that that was not the only reason the person was denied security clearance. They must say that they felt the person was not capable of doing the job, the person's health was not good enough, or they already had enough people.
This motion would ensure that in any circumstances in which the denial of a security clearance was a factor in firing, failing to hire, or failing to promote an individual, the review


Security Intelligence Service
process available under this Act would indeed be made available to the individual in question.
I know, or at least I would assume that the Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans), who represents a constituency in which there are many public servants, would support an amendment of this nature. I see him in the House now. I invite him to rise at the conclusion of my remarks to speak on behalf of the public servants whom he is supposed to represent on this important question. Or perhaps he will remain silent and refuse to speak on this amendment which would strengthen the protections of public servants who are denied promotions or fired from their jobs. Certainly his silence on this subject will be drawn to the attention of his constituents.
Another objective of these four motions is to ensure that in any circumstance in which there is a complaint about the denial of a security clearance or about some aspect of the operations of the Security Intelligence Review Committee, that complaint must be investigated. As it stands now, the review committee has the power to summarily dismiss, without even an investigation, a complaint if it is felt that the complainant is being, in their terms, frivolous, vexatious, or trivial. To dismiss a complaint even before a preliminary investigation on those grounds denies full and effective oversight and review of the operations of the Security Intelligence Review Committee.
There are other concerns with respect to the question of security assessments. I have noted the fantastic number of security assessments. I would like to quote again from Mr. Gordon Fairweather, the head of the Canadian Human Rights Commission. He said:
The unjustified proliferation of jobs for which a security assessment is required has a discriminatory impact, denying opportunities to persons of pardoned (criminal) conviction, national or ethnic origin, marital status or disability, all of which are prohibited grounds of discrimination under the Canadian Human Rights Act,-
Mr. Fairweather went on to say:
People who are denied jobs because of their sexual orientation or their political belief are discriminated against if the security check was never necessary in the first place.
Once again, those are areas in which the law should clearly be changed to reflect the desire, hopefully, of all Members of the House, not to discriminate on the grounds referred to by Mr. Fairweather in his comments on security checks.
In conclusion, I urge Members of the House to adopt the motion before the House with respect to the provisions on review, security clearances and the complaints process. I await with interest the contribution of the Member for Ottawa Centre who, as I indicated, is in the House today. I am sure he will want to rise on behalf of his constituents to support this amendment which would enhance the rights of public servants whom he is supposed to be representing.

Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to rise to speak on these motions, but after listening to the comments of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), I would like to make one or two related points. I certainly will not use the full time at my disposal.
It strikes me as being hopelessly naive at best to consider that many people will be advised that they have been refused employment on grounds of security. That is just not the way it happens in the real world. That is a sign of the kind of academic legal mind that this place abounds with which puts it so totally out of touch with reality. I am not knocking people in the legal profession. There are good and bad people, but some have a little more experience out in the real world than others. It does not happen that way in Government or in industry. The reason you are given for not getting a job, whether in government or private industry, may be reasons that touch on security, whether it be personal conduct or something else. The Government will have total access to this information. It can go into private medical records, legal records and tax records and there may be a host of reasons, not all of them illegal, that hold people open to some suspicion. It may be some activity in their past when they may not even have considered that they would be entering the employ of the Government. Young people in their teens often will get into scrapes that will be revealed in medical or other types of records but should have no bearing on it. It has certainly been my experience, both as a union representative and steward prior to coming to Parliament and certainly since being a Member of Parliament, that from the number of grievances coming from citizens, union members or people trying to get employee status with government or industry, one simply does not get those kinds of answers. It is absolutely unrealistic to believe that any government, whether it is Liberal, Conservative or NDP, can say that the reason that someone did not get a job is that he or she did not get national security clearance. That does not happen at all and will never happen.
A few weeks ago I was talking to a woman from Ainsworth, British Columbia, in my constituency. She talked about having discovered a black list from the mining industry in a cabin attached to another outbuilding behind her property. The list dates back half a century and it contained over 5,000 names from the Province of British Columbia. Unfortunately, it was treated as garbage and was thrown in the fire. That is a tragedy because there is nothing I would have liked better than to be able to produce a document such as that, because it was indicative of why the government and industry attempt not to hire people for a number of reasons. If the present Government or a future government continues with this economic trend, social tensions will likely become greater and provide further grounds for suspicion and for denying people status, and such powers will be exercised with increasing frequency.
During the McCarthy era in the 1950s, we know of dozens of people in the United States who made a career of drawing up "do not hire" lists for companies and governments. Not only did they make a business of drawing up those lists, they really made their money by allowing people to buy their name off the list when they found out that it would be included. Some people made a virtual career of that practice.
That is the sort of practice we are opening ourselves up to here, unless we allow this review process to be more flexible in


what it is allowed to review. These are very narrow and unrealistic specifications laid out by the Government in these clauses. I hope changes are made because these clauses do not reflect reality.

Motion No. 123
That Bill C-9 be amended by adding immediately after line 20 at page 24 the following:
