Mr. Speaker, there are some 40 clauses covered by these motions to delete clauses and it is those clauses to which I am addressing my remarks.
Without any doubt whatsoever, this Bill constitutes a massive assault on the most fundamental and basic civil liberties and rights to privacy of Canadians. The motions in question would delete a number of the most reprehensible provisions of this Bill. In the few minutes available to me, I would like to explain the purpose of these motions.
First, as the Bill now stands, the new civilian security service would have the power to massively invade the privacy of Canadians. It would have the unprecedented power to open first-class mail, to access confidential medical records and to examine confidential psychiatric records and journalists' records. Once again, I say that it is a disgrace and a shame that the press gallery is empty for this debate on one of the most important pieces of legislation in the country. Ironically, it may be the press that will become the victim of this new secret security service.
The service will have the power to break and enter anyone's home, to remove any document or indeed any thing from that home. In short, the powers that are proposed under the privisions of this Bill go far beyond those which were recommended by the McDonald Commission and have been attacked by virtually every witness that appeared before the Justice Committee. These witnesses included representatives from the Canadian Council of Churches, the Canadian Association of University Teachers, the Canadian Jewish Congress-I could go on and on. Yet the Government shamefully ignores the will of the people of the country and proposes to plough ahead with a piece of legislation which flies in the face of all of the traditions in this country of civil liberties and protection of fundamental rights and freedoms. Any member of that Government who can stand up and support this Bill should hang his head in shame, because he is prepared to be a party to this attack on the civil liberties and the rights to privacy of Canadians.
The Bill constitutes nothing less than a denial of the rule of law in the country. There are those who ask if this is not at least a step forward because they say the status quo is not adequate. To them I say no, a thousand times no. While the status quo is flawed, this Bill with its sweeping mandate to target Canadians who have broken no laws whatsoever, this Bill with its wide and unprecedented powers to invade the privacy of Canadians, this Bill which denies Parliament a fundamental role to play in the oversight of the operations of the security service in the country, is a Bill which must be rejected by this Parliament if we are to preserve democracy in the country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to assure you that I look forward to a full and productive evening. However, I want to draw to your attention Standing Order 15(2) which states:
When the Speaker is putting a question, no Member shall enter, walk out of or across the House, or make any noise or disturbance.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Let us not talk about the noise or disturbance, but I believe I saw a certain government Member walk in and out of the House. I do not think that vote should be counted with respect to this matter. It was improper and should not be allowed.

Mr. Speaker, I hope you did not record the votes of the Members for Yukon, Calgary Centre, Vancouver Centre and Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Nielsen, Mr. Andre, Miss Carney and Mr. Dick). The first three left the House during the division and the last Hon. Member was not in his seat.

A Member must be in his own seat should he wish to vote and should remain in his seat until the division is complete and the result announced.

Mr. Speaker, may I put a proposition to you? I think we are making some progress in terms of the question of deferred votes as opposed to consequential votes. The government House Leader has indicated that all votes are completely covered on the basis of deferral. I would put it to you, Mr. Speaker, that on the basis of the vote on Motion No. 42, if that vote were in fact negatived, it would then require that we have a vote on Motion No. 43. This is the first time that Motion No. 43 will come before the House for deliberation and voting. The conventional way of dealing with a motion which has not been voted on before and which is only consequential to certain negative results on Motion No. 42 is that you place the question to the House on a voice vote. This is the normal procedure.
The point I am making, Mr. Speaker, is that this is the first time this question has been considered by the House. It is not a matter of dealing with an affirmative result on Motion No. 42 which would then deal with subsequent motions. We are dealing with a specific direction given by Your Honour with respect to groupings. I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the question of the ringing of the bell is a matter which the House would have to decide depending upon the rules of the House. In that circumstance, there is the provision for five Members to cause the division bells to ring. We are coming up to No. 47 and I am concerned about the practices we are following here. I am suggesting that when the Chair calls Motion No. 47, the correct practice should be for the Chair to call for the yeas and nays and cause a voice division.
I can tell the Government House Leader now that we are prepared, in advance, to respond positively to the usual request of the Chair when the Chair calls for the yeas and nays and declares the winner of the voice division. The Chair then normally asks whether it should dispense with the ringing of the bells. If that question is put, I can tell you, on behalf of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, that our response would be positive and we will dispense with the bells. I am concerned with the practice.
I submit to you, with all the strength at my command, that the practice which I have described here is the proper one backed up by all sorts of precedents in the House. I would suggest that you put the question in that fashion and cause the voice division. I can tell you that there will be no intentional bell ringing as far as we in Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition are concerned. I cannot speak for all Members because, of course, any five Members can rise to cause that actual recorded division.

The task of the Chair is not an easy one. After midnight it gets more difficult. I can only observe that the Chair acted in terms of its own recollection. During the break a check was made. Clearly there are more precedents in the direction indicated by the Hon. Member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) and Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn) than in terms of the recollection of the present occupant of the Chair. In terms of the record of the majority of instances in the House there has been a voice vote called in such circumstances. The Chair obviously has certain difficulties at this point. Perhaps the House can show a little generosity. We will proceed with a voice vote at this point.
